en: An auspicious beginning:
The Patañjala Yoga Sūtra,
together with the Rājamārtaṇḍa commentary composed by Bhojadeva, the Lord of Dhārā.

May that union of the two halves of the body of Śiva and Śivā bestow blessings upon you—by the mere remembrance of which a person attains liberation (kaivalya), though it is otherwise difficult to reach;
and by the recollection of which the three kinds of suffering of men [are destroyed]. 1.1–2ab.
We praise that immutable Śiva, who instantly brings about dissolution;
victorious is this unprecedented utterance of the sage Patañjali, by which even the separation of the Spirit (puruṣa) and Nature (prakṛti) is declared to be Yoga. 2–3.
Victorious are the words of the Lord of Serpents (Patañjali), which possess the luster of the moon dispelling the mass of inner darkness;
when contemplated, they constantly render the minds of the virtuous ever-filled with bliss.
(4) While composing the *Pātañjala* [Mahābhāṣya], which provides the instruction on words...

Victorious are the brilliant words of His Majesty King Raṇaraṅgamalla, by whom— even while composing the medical treatise known as the *Rājamṛgāṅka*— the impurity of speech, mind, and body was extracted, just as the Lord of Serpents [Śeṣa] upholds the earth. 5.

They abandon that which is exceedingly difficult to understand with the claim that it is "of clear meaning," yet they provide excessive elaboration for what is already clear through useless compounds and the like; thus, by means of many irrelevant and misplaced prattlings, they spread confusion.

"Of the listeners"—thus [he speaks], for all commentators have brought about a distortion of the subject matter. Setting aside prolixity, casting away the web of conceptual constructions, and having correctly ascertained the meanings that are revealed with little clarity; ||6||
This exposition of the internal doctrine of Patañjali is being set forth by me as a means for the awakening of wise people.
(7) Samādhipāda.
Now begins the first chapter on concentration (samādhi-pāda):
Now follows the instruction on yoga (yogānuśāsana).
Commentary on the First Sūtra: By this sūtra, the connection, subject matter, and purpose of the treatise are explained;
furthermore, the word *atha* indicates the commencement of the topic and serves as an auspicious invocation.

Yoga is reasoning, it is concentration; since the root *yuj* means "to concentrate," that by which one is instructed— that is, explained— through its definitions, divisions, means, and fruits, is *anuśāsana* (instruction).
The "instruction on yoga" (yogānuśāsana) means that [this] is to be understood as the governing principle from here until the completion of the treatise. In this context,
since it is the subject to be explained by the treatise, yoga— along with its means and its results— is the subject matter (*abhidheya*).
The exposition of that [yoga] is the purpose; the fruit of the yoga thus explained is liberation (kaivalya);
and the relationship between the scripture and its subject matter is characterized by that of the expositor and the exposited.
The relationship of means and end between the subject matter and its result, which is isolation (*kaivalya*), is as follows:
what is intended is this—the means for the yoga to be mastered are demonstrated by the treatise;
yoga, once established through those means, produces the result known as isolation.
Regarding this, he asks: "What is yoga? and replies:
"Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind."
The second [definition of] *samādhi*:

The modifications (*vṛtti*) of the mind—which consists of the transformation into pure *sattva*—are themselves transformations in the form of the relationship between primary and subordinate factors. The cessation (*nirodha*) of these [modifications], through the interruption of their outward-directed transformation and by means of an inward-directed reverse transformation, is their dissolution into their own cause; this is designated as *yoga*.
Furthermore, this cessation is a property (*dharma*) common to all levels of consciousness (*cittabhūmi*) and to all living beings, though it manifests at some time on some particular level.

And these are the stages (*bhūmi*) of the mind—specific states of the mind—namely: the distracted (*kṣipta*), the stupefied (*mūḍha*), the scattered (*vikṣipta*), the one-pointed (*ekāgra*), and the restrained (*niruddha*).

Among these, the "distracted" is unstable due to the predominance of *rajas*; being outward-turned, it is impelled by *rajas* toward objects such as pleasure and pain, whether they are conceptualized or remote;
and this state belongs constantly to the Daityas, Dānavas, and others.

The deluded state, due to the predominance of *tamas*, is restricted solely to contrary actions such as anger and the like, without any distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
this state belongs eternally to *rakṣasas*, *piśācas*, and similar beings.
The distracted state, however, due to the predominance of *sattva*, specifically avoids the means of suffering and engages only with the objects of pleasure, such as sound and the rest.
And this always applies to the gods;
it is said as follows: through *rajas* the mind takes the form of activity, through *tamas* it is intent on harming others, and through *sattva* it becomes composed of happiness.
These three states of mind are useless for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The two qualities of *sattva* and *rajas*, in the form of one-pointedness and restraint respectively, serve a purpose in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) because they are established in an ascending order of excellence.

As for the reversal of the sequence beginning with *sattva*, the intention is as follows: although both *rajas* and *tamas* are ultimately to be abandoned, *rajas* is mentioned first for this specific purpose;
for as long as "activity" (*pravṛtti*) has not been demonstrated, "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) cannot be shown. Thus, the two are presented in reverse order.

However, this is shown later for the sake of the practitioner (*sattva*): that by means of its excellence, the two subsequent stages are conducive to yoga. Thus, it is stated that yoga is the transformation of the mind into one-pointedness within these two stages—one-pointedness and cessation—wherein there is the cessation of outward mental fluctuations in the state of one-pointedness.
And when all functions have ceased and there is the dissolution of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the possibility of yoga exists only in these two stages.
Now, the author of the Sūtras, desiring to explain the terms for the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*), first explains the term "mind" (*citta*).
Then, the seer abides in his own nature; this is samādhi. [The commentary states:
At that time, the seer—the Puruṣa—abides, meaning he remains established, in his own nature, which is pure consciousness alone.

The meaning is this: because there is no transfer of consciousness (*citsaṃkrama*) for one in whom discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen, the conceit of agency ceases; when the intellect (*buddhi*) has its modifications extinguished, the Self’s abiding in its own nature constitutes "stability" (*sthiti*).
But what is its form during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)? To this he says:
"In other cases, concentration is conformity with the modifications.
"Modification"—in "other cases," that is, at times other than yoga, there are modifications whose characteristics will be described hereafter; "conformity" with these means having their same form.
This is the meaning: whatever kinds of fluctuations—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—arise, the Puruṣa is perceived by the agents of worldly experience as being of that very same form.

Thus, when the power of consciousness (citiśakti) becomes established in its own nature through transformation into one-pointedness, and when it transforms into the form of an object by means of the fluctuations of the senses, the Puruṣa appears as if it were of that very form; just as when the waves of water move, the moon appears to be moving. That is the mind (citta).
To explain the term "modes of functioning" (vṛtti), he says:
"The modes of functioning are fivefold, being either afflicted or unafflicted."
Commentary on Sūtra 5: "Mental modifications" (*vṛttayaḥ*) are specific transformations of the mind (*citta*).

The suffix *-taya* (in *vṛttayaḥ*) is used in reference to those modifications which constitute the parts of the whole (*avayavin*) characterized by the collection of modifications. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.42)
2.42) This is what is meant: of what nature are the five modes of functioning?
Defiled (kliṣṭa) means overcome by the afflictions (kleśa) whose characteristics will be explained below;
those contrary to that are undefiled (akliṣṭa).
These same five fluctuations are now stated concisely:
valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory.
Commentary on the sixth [chapter on] Samādhi: He states the definition of these [means of knowledge] in their proper order—
perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas).

Commentary on Samādhi 7: Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are so well-known here, and since their definition has already been established by the author of the treatise through the determination of their divisions, no separate definition has been provided.
However, the definition of the means of valid cognition is as follows: "Non-contradictory cognition is the means of valid cognition."

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the mind, primarily characterized by the determination of the specific features of an object—which consists of both general and particular aspects—due to its coloring by an external thing through the door of the sense organs.
Inference (*anumāna*) is the ascertainment of a general property in the subject (*liṅgin*) based on a mark (*liṅga*) whose relationship [to that property] has been previously apprehended.
Verbal testimony (*āgama*) is the word of a reliable authority (*āpta*).

Having thus explained the functioning characterized by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states that characterized by error (*viparyaya*): "Error is false knowledge, not established in the form of that [object]."
Commentary on Samādhi 8: Error (*viparyaya*) is knowledge arising with respect to an object that is not as it appears;
for example, the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

"Not established in that form" means that it does not rest upon the form which is the actual nature of that object; that is to say, it does not manifest the ultimate (pāramārthika) form of that object.
Even doubt is a false cognition (mithyājñāna) because it is not established in that [true] form.
In order to explain the function of conceptual construction (*vikalpavṛtti*), he says: "For example, 'Is it a post or a person? (8)
"Vikalpa is a mental modification that follows verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object.
(YS 1.9) — "Verbal knowledge" (śabdajñāna) is the cognition produced by words.

That which has the nature of following after that [verbal cognition] is called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); it is a mental determination (*adhyavasāya*) that follows verbal knowledge while disregarding the actual state of the object,
such as "consciousness is the essential nature of the person."

In this regard, when the cognition "Devadatta’s blanket" arises from the word, the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) proceeds by superimposing that distinction—which is determined by the genitive case—even though it does not exist here;
for in reality, the person (*puruṣa*) is nothing but consciousness alone.
To explain sleep, he says: "Sleep is a mental modification (vṛtti) that has the absence of objects as its support; it is a [type of] samādhi. (YS 1.10)
Commentary: That whose objective support (*ālambana*) is the cognition of non-existence is so described.
This is what is meant: that mental modification (*vṛtti*) which proceeds by abandoning all objects due to the constant intensification of darkness is sleep (*nidrā*).
And because we observe the memory, "I slept happily," and because memory is impossible without a prior experience, it follows that sleep is indeed a mental modification.
To explain mindfulness (smṛti), he says:
mindfulness is the non-forgetting of an experienced object.

Commentary on Samādhi 11: That which is the non-forgetting of an object experienced through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its re-ascension into the intellect by way of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), is memory (*smṛti*).
Among these, the means of valid cognition, error (*viparyaya*), and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) belong to the waking state.
These very [mental states], being attenuated by the force of that experience, become dream;
sleep, however, is a state where objects are not consciously perceived;
and memory arises from the causes of valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, and sleep.

Having thus explained the fluctuations (*vṛtti*), he speaks in order to explain their cessation along with its means: "Their cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion. (*abhyāsavairāgyābhyāṃ tannirodhaḥ*)

Commentary on Sūtra 12: It has been stated that through practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*), whose definitions will be explained later, there occurs the cessation of those mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which consist of illumination, activity, and restraint.
When these modifications—having turned away from their external attachments—are directed inward, they abide within the mind itself, their own cause, in the form of latent potential (*śakti*).
In this regard, aversion toward those objects is produced by detachment born from perceiving their defects,
and firm stability is produced through practice by means of demonstrating a peaceful flow that generates happiness;
thus, by these two, the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind occurs.
To explain practice (abhyāsa), he says: "In that regard, effort toward steadiness is practice."

Commentary on Sūtra 13: Stability (*sthiti*) is the transformation of the mind, which is free from fluctuations (*vṛtti*), that abides in its own true nature. Effort (*yatna*) toward that stability is enthusiasm; the repeated settling of the mind in that state is called practice (*abhyāsa*).
He states its specific distinction:
"But that concentration, when practiced for a long time, with devotion, without interruption, and with reverence, becomes firmly established. (14)
Commentary: When practiced for a long time, continuously, and with great reverence, it becomes firmly established; that is to say, it becomes stable and capable of attaining firmness.
He states the definition of dispassion (vairāgya):
"Dispassion is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard" (Yoga Sūtra 1.15).
Commentary: For the object of experience is indeed twofold—the perceived and the scriptural.
The perceived is that which is apprehended right here in this world, such as sound and so forth; the scriptural is that which pertains to the world of the gods and other such realms.
That which is heard from the mouth of the teacher is *anuśrava*; the Veda is so called because it has come from that, and what originates from it is *ānuśravika*.

When one has become free from greed due to seeing the lack of relish in the transformation of both these objects of experience, there arises the consciousness of mastery (*vaśīkārasaṃjñā*)—this reflection, "These are under my control; I am not under their control"—is called detachment (*vairāgya*).
He states its specific distinction: "That supreme [samādhi] is freedom from craving for the guṇas resulting from the discernment of the Puruṣa. (Yoga Sūtra 1.16)

Commentary: That dispassion is supreme and preeminent. The first [type of] dispassion has objects as its domain; the second has the *guṇas* as its domain. It arises only from the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) of the evolved *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*, because it is extremely conducive to the *nirodha-samādhi*.

Having thus described the essential nature of yoga, he states the distinctions within the nature of *samprajñāta* [cognitive] concentration: "Cognitive concentration is that which is accompanied by the forms of reasoning (*vitarka*), reflection (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*). (YS 1.17)
Commentary: "Samādhi" is the understood remainder of the sentence.
That by which the form of the object of meditation (*bhāvya*) is correctly—meaning free from doubt and error—and thoroughly known is *samprajñāta* samādhi, a specific type of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
It is fourfold, distinguished as having *vitarka* and so forth: namely, with *vitarka*, with *vicāra*, with *ānanda*, and with *asmitā*.

Meditation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated placement of the mind upon the object of meditation (*bhāvya*) by means of abandoning other objects; and the object of meditation is twofold: the Lord (*īśvara*) and the principles (*tattva*).
These [principles] are also twofold, due to the distinction between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*).
The twenty-four principles are insentient, while the Puruṣa is sentient.

Among these, when meditation is performed by taking the gross elements and the senses as objects, through the synthesis of preceding and succeeding moments and the blending of the mental impression with the verbal designation of the object, then that is *samādhi* with deliberation (*savitarka*).

When meditation proceeds upon this very object of focus, devoid of the mental verbalization (*śabdollekha*) that links the preceding with the succeeding, it is then "without deliberation" (*nirvitarka*).

When meditation is performed upon a subtle object—characterized by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—by way of its delimitation through space, time, and qualities (*dharma*), it is then "with deliberation" (*savicāra*).

Meditation performed upon that same object of focus, without the delimitation of space, time, and qualities, and appearing as the substrate alone (*dharmimātra*), is called "without deliberation" (*nirvicāra*).
Samādhi reaching this limit is designated as "grasping absorption" (grāhyasamāpatti).

However, when the *sattva* of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is cultivated while still permeated by traces of *rajas* and *tamas*, then, due to the predominance of that cultivated *sattva*—which consists of bliss and luminosity over the state of the qualities (*guṇa*)—there arises "samādhi with bliss" (*sānanda-samādhi*).

Those who, being fixed in that very samādhi, do not perceive the other principle consisting of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, are designated by the term "bodiless" (*videha*), because they are free from the ego-identification with the body.
This is the attainment of apprehension (*grahaṇa-samāpatti*).

Beyond that, when one takes as an object pure *sattva* that is no longer overwhelmed by even a trace of *rajas* and *tamas*, the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that proceeds therein is called "with self-consciousness" (*sāsmita*), because the object of cognition has subsided and the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) has become predominant, such that only pure existence remains.
Furthermore, one should not suspect that there is no difference between egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and self-consciousness (*asmitā*).
That wherein the internal organ perceives objects through the manifestation of "I" is *ahaṃkāra* (ego).

That wherein, through inward-turnedness and the reverse process of transformation, mere existence (*sattāmātra*) shines forth when the mind has dissolved into its source (*prakṛti*), is *asmitā* (the sense of "I-am-ness"). Those who find satisfaction in this very *samādhi* and do not perceive the Supreme Self, the Puruṣa, are said to be "dissolved into *prakṛti*" (*prakṛtilaya*) when their minds have merged into their own cause.
For those who, having known the Supreme Puruṣa, proceed with meditative cultivation, this discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is called the "attainment of the grasper" (*grahītṛ-samāpatti*).
In that cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*), four stages persist in the form of latent potencies;
the abandonment of each one occurs successively in the following stages. Thus, this cognitive concentration consists of four stages.
He describes the state of non-cognitive [samādhi]: "The other samādhi, preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation, has only residual impressions remaining. 18.
Commentary: That by which one ceases is "cessation" (*virāma*), which is the abandonment of thoughts such as *vitarka* and so forth;
this cessation is itself the "cognition" (*pratyaya*), hence it is "the cognition of cessation" (*virāma-pratyaya*).
Its "practice" (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated fixing of that [cognition] in the mind.

In that state, whatever mental modification (*vṛtti*) arises, its continuous negation by means of "not this, not this" (*neti neti*)—the practice of the thought of cessation—is the *samprajñāta-samādhi* preceded by that;
the other, which is distinct from that and remains as a residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*), is the *asamprajñāta-samādhi*. This is the meaning.
Therein, nothing whatsoever is cognizable;
this is the seedless (nirbīja) samādhi known as "non-discerning" (asamprajñāta).
Here, there are four kinds of transformation of the mind: emergence (vyutthāna), the commencement of samādhi, one-pointedness (ekāgratā), and cessation (nirodha).

Among those, the stages of the distracted and the dull-witted minds constitute the stage of emergence; the stage of the scattered mind is the commencement of meditative concentration due to the predominance of sattva;
and the stages of cessation and one-pointedness are the final stages.

And with each transformation, the formative impressions (saṃskāras) therein are countered: the formative impressions produced by emergence are countered by those born from the commencement of meditative concentration (samādhi),
and those born from that [concentration] are countered by those born from one-pointedness.
The formative forces (*saṃskāra*) born of cessation— which arise from one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*)— destroy both themselves and [the other] formative forces.
Just as lead, when smelted together with gold, consumes both itself and the impurities of the gold,
so too do the formative forces born of cessation consume the formative forces produced by one-pointedness and themselves as well.
Having thus briefly stated the nature, the divisions, and the means of yoga, he now begins to explain the means in detail, preceded by a demonstration of the practice of yoga:
"For those who are merged in the bodyless [elements] and in primordial matter (prakṛti), [the attainment of yoga] is conditioned by their state of existence."

Commentary on Samādhi 19: Those who are bodiless (*videha*) and those who are dissolved into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) have been explained in the Sūtra on the Stages of Vitarka and the Others (1.17).
Their meditative absorption (*samādhi*) has existence as its condition;
"existence" (*bhava*) means *saṃsāra*, and that which has this as its condition or cause is "conditioned by existence.
The meaning is this: even while remaining within the highest degree [of the preparatory stage], they come to possess such meditative absorption within *saṃsāra*.
Because they do not perceive the supreme reality, this is merely a semblance of yoga;
therefore, for one who desires liberation, great effort must be applied toward the knowledge of the supreme reality and its cultivation—this is what has been taught.
But for others, however— namely, for the rest, concentration is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. 20.

Commentary: For those other than those who have attained the state of bodiless liberation (*videha*) or absorption into primordial matter (*prakṛtilaya*), [the means] is preceded by faith and so forth—that is, that which has faith and the rest as its prior means.
And these, beginning with faith, proceeding in sequence as the relationship between means and end, attain the status of being the means to *samprajñāta* concentration.
Among them, faith (*śraddhā*) is the clarity of the mind regarding the subject of yoga.
Vigor is enthusiasm;
mindfulness is the non-forgetting of what has been experienced;
concentration is one-pointedness.
Wisdom is the discernment of that which is to be known;
in one who possesses faith, vigor arises, and being enthusiastic regarding the object of yoga, one becomes possessed of energy;
and for one who possesses energy, mindfulness arises in the subsequent stages.
And through that remembrance, the mind becomes concentrated;
with a concentrated mind, one understands the object of meditation through correct discernment.
These are the means for cognitive (*samprajñāta*) concentration; from its practice and from supreme dispassion (*vairāgya*), non-cognitive (*asamprajñāta*) concentration arises.
He states the distinctions among yogins who possess the aforementioned means, based on the differences in those means:
"For those with intense ardor, [the result] is near."
Commentary on Samādhi 21: The phrase "attainment of samādhi" is to be understood as the remainder [of the definition].
*Saṃvega* is a more firmly established latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that serves as the cause for action.
For those whose means are intense, the attainment of meditative concentration is near, and the fruit of that concentration is also near;
the meaning is that it is accomplished very quickly.
Who are those of intense spiritual urgency (*tīvrasaṃvega*)? He says:
"Because of being weak, middling, or superior, there is even a further distinction from that [intensity] regarding meditative absorption (*samādhi*). (22)

Commentary: From those means, which are distinguished by the divisions of weak and so forth, there arises a distinction among those possessing the means—namely, weak, middling, and intense; these are the divisions of the means.
Each of these is further threefold, according to the distinctions of weak intensity, middling intensity, and intense intensity.
And according to their distinctions, there are nine types of practitioners: those with weak means, weak intensity, medium intensity, and intense intensity;
those with medium means, weak intensity, medium intensity, and intense intensity;
and those with superior means, weak intensity, medium intensity, and intense intensity.
The instruction on the distinction [of methods] is that great effort must be exerted regarding superior means and intense spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
Now, in order to show another method that is easy to practice and distinct from this [previous] method, he says:
Or, from devotion to the Lord, concentration arises.
(Yoga Sūtra 1.23) Commentary: The Lord is defined by the characteristics that will be described hereafter.
In this context, *praṇidhāna* is a special devotion, distinguished worship, and the dedication of all actions to Him;
desiring no fruit such as sensual pleasure, one dedicates all actions to that Supreme Teacher.
That *praṇidhāna* is the excellent means for both meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the attainment of its fruit.
It has been stated that the attainment of *samādhi* results from devotion to God (*īśvara*).
Regarding this, he speaks as follows to explain, in due order, the nature of God, His authority, His power, His designator, the method of worship, and its fruit:
The Lord (Īśvara) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (kleśa), actions (karman), their fruitions (vipāka), or latent dispositions (āśaya).
Regarding the function [of this definition]: "afflictions" (kleśa) refers to ignorance (avidyā) and the others that will be described hereafter, so called because they afflict.
Actions are of the nature of being prescribed, prohibited, or mixed;
they ripen, and thus "ripenings" (*vipāka*) are the fruits of action consisting of birth, lifespan, and experience.
Because they lie within the ground of the mind until the ripening of their fruit, they are called "disposition" (*āśaya*), which is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as *vāsanā*.

Untouched by those [afflictions] and not contacted at any of the three times, the "distinguished person" (*puruṣaviśeṣa*) is distinguished from other persons; thus he is the "Distinguished One" (*viśeṣa*), the Lord (*īśvara*). He is characterized by sovereignty, capable of uplifting the entire world by mere will.
Although all selves (*ātman*) are untouched by afflictions and the like, nevertheless, those [afflictions] residing in the mind are attributed to them [as if they were their own].
Just as victory and defeat belonging to the warriors belong to their master,
yet for this [Lord], there is no such conceptualization of afflictions and so forth in any of the three times;
therefore, the Blessed Lord Īśvara is indeed distinct from them.
And his such sovereignty arises from the excellence of his being (*sattva*), which itself arises from preeminent knowledge; furthermore,
there is no mutual dependence between this knowledge and sovereignty, because they are independent of one another.
Those two—knowledge and sovereignty—reside in the *sattva* of the Lord and are beginningless; therefore, His connection with that kind of *sattva* is indeed beginningless.
This is because the conjunction and disjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are not possible apart from the will of the Lord.

Just as the mind of other living beings—which has transformed into the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—becomes an object of experience when it is reflected in the pure *sattva* (which is characterized by the manifestation of virtue) through the transfer of the shadow of consciousness (*cicchāyā*), it is not so for the Lord.
For him, there exists only a purely sattvic transformation, characterized by excellence and established as an object of experience through a beginningless connection;
therefore, by virtue of being distinct from other puruṣas, he alone is the Lord (Īśvara).
In the case of liberated souls (muktātman), however, the repeated association with afflictions and the like has been removed by various means taught in the scriptures.
Furthermore, because this [Self] is always of such a nature, it does not possess equality with liberated souls;
nor is there a plurality of Lords, for if they were equal, their intentions would differ, and thus the production of any single effect would be impossible.
Regarding the state of being endowed with increase and decrease, he who is the most excellent is indeed the Lord (Īśvara), because sovereignty reaches its ultimate limit in him alone.
In that regard, the unsurpassed seed of omniscience is the function of meditative absorption (samādhi).

Within that Blessed One, that which is the seed of omniscience— the smallness or greatness of the grasping of the past, future, and so forth— is called the "seed" because, being the root, it is like a seed.
Therefore, that [Brahman] is there unsurpassed and has reached its ultimate limit;
for we observe that qualities such as smallness and greatness, which possess degrees of excellence, reach their ultimate limit— for instance,
smallness in an atom and supreme greatness in space.
In this way, mental qualities such as knowledge and the rest, being observed to exist in varying degrees of intensity, reach a state of unsurpassed excellence somewhere;
and he in whom these are unsurpassed is the Lord (Īśvara).

Although it is not possible to comprehend His specific attributes because inference terminates at the general level alone, nevertheless, His specific attributes such as omniscience and so forth are to be understood from scripture (śāstra).

One should not raise the doubt as to how He brings about the union and separation of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* in the absence of any personal motive of His own; for, being compassionate, His sole motive is the favoring of living beings.
His resolve is: "I shall deliver all transmigrating souls without exception at the end of the kalpa, the dissolution of the world, and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).
Whatever is desired by Him is His motive.
Having thus stated the proof for the Lord, he now declares His power:
"He is the teacher even of the ancients, because He is not limited by time."
Commentary on Samādhi 26: He is the teacher and instructor even of the primordial creators, such as Brahmā and others, because he is not limited by time due to his beginninglessness;
whereas for those such as Brahmā, there is a limitation by time because they possess a beginning.
Having thus described its power, he states the designator for the purpose of its worship:
"Its designator is the syllable Om (praṇava)."

Commentary on Sūtra 27: Of this Lord whose nature has been thus described, the *praṇava*—the syllable *oṃ*—is the designator (*vācaka*) and the signifier (*abhidhāyaka*), because by means of it one is praised (*nūyate*) or extolled (*stūyate*) pre-eminently, or because it praises (*nauti*) or extols (*stauti*).

Furthermore, the relationship between these two, characterized as that of the signified and the signifier, is eternal; it is manifested through convention (*saṃketa*), but it is not created by anyone.
Just as the existing relationship between father and son is made manifest by someone [saying], "This is his father; this is his son," [the text] states the method of worship:
Upāsanam āha— (He states the meditation:)

The commentary on verse 28: *tajjapaḥ tadarthabhāvanam samādhiḥ*—"The repetition (*japa*) of that [syllable], which consists of three and a half measures (*mātrā*), is its correct pronunciation; and the contemplation (*bhāvana*) of its denoted object, the Lord, is the repeated fixing of Him in the mind. This is the means for achieving one-pointedness."
Therefore, it is stated that for the sake of attaining samādhi, the yogin should mutter the praṇava and meditate upon its referent, the Lord (Īśvara).
[28] He now states the fruit of this practice:
Thence arises the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles; this is the function of samādhi (29).
That is to say, from that repetition [of the mantra] and from the contemplation of its meaning, the yogin attains the realization of the inward-turned consciousness.

The consciousness that turns inward toward one's own internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) due to aversion toward sense objects—that power of vision is "inward-directed consciousness" (pratyak-cetanā). The meaning is that the attainment of that is knowledge.
The obstacles will be described later;
their absence constitutes the removal of impediments to that power.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the obstacles (antarāya) are, he says:

illness, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of dispassion, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage [of concentration], and instability—these distractions of the mind are the obstacles.
Commentary on Sūtra 30: These nine, proceeding from the force of *rajas* and *tamas*, become distractions of the mind;
the meaning is that the mind is distracted by these [states] which are opposed to one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).
In that context, "disease" refers to fever and the like caused by an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*);
"stupefaction" is the mind's lack of functional capacity;
"doubt" is a cognition whose object consists of two opposing alternatives—for instance, whether or not yoga is to be accomplished.
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is a lack of attentiveness, an indifference toward the means for achieving meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
and laziness (*ālasya*), which is a heaviness of body and mind that serves as the cause for the absence of engagement with the object of yoga.
Non-restraint (*avirati*) is a craving characterized by the mind’s association with sense objects.

Delusory perception is erroneous cognition, such as [perceiving] silver in mother-of-pearl; not having attained the stages refers to the non-attainment or failure to acquire the stages of meditative concentration due to some cause;
and instability refers to the mind's lack of firm establishment upon those stages even after they have been attained.
These are called obstacles because they are, as the case may be, the opposites of one-pointedness of concentration.
To demonstrate other obstacles as well that cause distraction of the mind, he says:
Suffering, dejection, bodily restlessness, and inhalation and exhalation are co-existent with distraction; this is the function of concentration (samādhi).
When distractions arise from some cause, these factors—suffering and the rest—come into operation.
Among these, *duḥkha* (pain) is a transformation of the mind characterized by *rajas*, having the nature of affliction; because of this affliction, living beings act for its own destruction.
*Daurmanasya* (dejection) is the mental distress caused by external and internal factors.
*Aṅgamejayatva* (trembling of the limbs) is a shaking of all the limbs that obstructs stability of posture and mind.
When one inhales the external air, that is inhalation (*śvāsa*); when one exhales the abdominal air, that is exhalation (*praśvāsa*).
These, occurring along with distractions, are to be restrained by means of the practice and dispassion already described; such is the instruction regarding them.
He states another means for the purpose of preventing those obstacles and distractions:
"For the sake of preventing them, the practice of a single principle is *samādhi*. (3.2)
Commentary: For the purpose of restraining those distractions, one should practice the repeated application of the mind to some single, chosen reality;
by the power of which, when one-pointedness has arisen, those distractions go to their destruction.
Now, he states another means for the cultivation that brings about the mental formations [of concentration]:

"The clarification of the mind through the cultivation of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, directed toward objects that are happy, miserable, virtuous, and non-virtuous, is samādhi. (33)
Commentary: Maitrī is friendliness;
karuṇā is compassion;
muditā is joy.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is indifference;
one should cultivate these [four immeasurables] respectively toward those who are happy, those who are suffering, those who possess merit, and those who lack merit.
For instance, toward virtuous people who are happy, one should practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*), thinking, "How wonderful that they are happy," rather than practicing envy.
Toward those who are suffering, one should cultivate only compassion, thinking, "How indeed might their suffering come to an end? rather than maintaining indifference.

Toward those possessing merit, one should feel joy through the sympathetic rejoicing in their merit, rather than feeling resentment by wondering, "Why are these people meritorious? And toward those lacking merit, one should cultivate equanimity alone, neither rejoicing nor feeling hatred.
In the sūtras, those who possess happiness, suffering, and so forth are indicated by the words "happiness," "suffering," and so on.
Thus, when the mind becomes serene through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], concentration manifests through ease;
and this cultivation constitutes external action.

Just as in arithmetic, operations such as addition and so forth serve as auxiliaries for the completion of the calculation of mixed numbers and the like, thereby contributing to the accomplishment of the primary task; even so, a mind that has produced clarity through the cultivation of friendliness (*maitrī*) and other qualities—which serve as antidotes to hatred, passion, and the rest—becomes fit for concentrations such as *samprajñāta*.
For it is passion and hatred alone that primarily give rise to distraction;
if these two were uprooted along with their very roots, then, due to the serenity of the mind, one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) arises.
He states another means:
"Or [it is accomplished] by means of the expulsion and retention of the vital breath."
Commentary on Samādhi 34:
*Pracchardana* is the expulsion of the abdominal air from the body to a specific measure by means of a particular effort;
*vidhāraṇā* is the cessation of the outward movement of the vital air (*prāṇa*) for that same measure of time.
And that [breath-control] occurs in two ways: by filling the internal [space] with the external [air], or by the cessation of that which has already been filled right there.

Thus, breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is threefold—exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka)—and it binds the mind’s stability to one-pointedness. This is because all modifications of the senses are preceded by the modifications of the vital breath (prāṇa), and because the mind and the vital breath share a common fate regarding their respective functions. When the vital breath is conquered, it becomes capable of establishing the mind in one-pointedness through the cessation of the modifications of all the senses.
Furthermore, it is heard in the scriptures that this [practice] brings about the destruction of all defects,
and since all distracted mental states are produced by defects,
it possesses the capacity for one-pointedness even by means of the removal of those defects.
Now, by introducing another means, he describes a preliminary limb of conscious concentration (samprajñāta-samādhi):
"Or, an activity directed toward an object, when it has arisen, brings about stability."
Commentary on Sūtra 35: "Of the mind"—this is the remainder of the sentence.
That activity which possesses objects—namely, smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—as its fruits is called "object-possessing" (*viṣayavatī*); such activity brings about stability of the mind.
For instance, for one who fixes the mind on the tip of the nose, a perception of divine fragrance arises; likewise, on the tip of the tongue there is a perception of taste,
and on the tip of the palate, a perception of form.
In the middle of the tongue there is the consciousness of touch,
and at the root of the tongue there is the consciousness of sound;

thus, the consciousness arising through the respective doors of those various sense organs regarding their respective objects, being divine in nature, becomes the cause for one-pointedness of the mind.
"There is a fruit of yoga," [he says], because this produces confidence in the yogin.
Thus he states another such means:

The state of concentration (samādhi) called "the sorrowless" or "the luminous" is a mental modification (vṛtti); the completion of the sentence is that this modification, once arisen, brings about stability of the mind.
By the word "light" (jyotis), sattvic illumination is meant; that activity which possesses such illumination—being praiseworthy, abundant, and preeminent—is called "luminous" (jyotiṣmatī).

It is "free from sorrow" (viśokā), meaning that sorrow, which is a transformation of rajas, has departed due to the power of practicing sattva, which consists of happiness; thus it binds the mind to steadiness.

This is the meaning: for one who meditates on the *sattva* of the mind within the hollow center of the heart-lotus as resembling the ocean of milk with its waves completely stilled, stability of the mind arises through the light of wisdom upon the cessation of all mental fluctuations (YS 1.36).
By way of demonstrating another means, he shows the object of *samprajñāta-samādhi*:
Or, a mind whose object is one free from passion becomes a basis for the stability of the mind;
this is the remainder [of the sentence]. (37) Commentary: It remains to be understood that it serves as a cause for the steadiness of the mind.

One who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) has abandoned the desire for sense objects; his mind, being devoid of afflictions (*kleśa*), when taken as an object of focus, becomes the cause for the stability of the mind.
Thus, he states another such means:
Or, concentration (samādhi) has as its object the cognition of dream or sleep.
Regarding the commentary: when the functions of the external senses have subsided, that state in which the self experiences the state of being an enjoyer by means of the mind alone is called "dream."
Sleep, characterized as previously described,
when its object— whether the object of a dream or the object of sleep itself— is taken as the support for knowledge, brings about stability of the mind. 38
Because living beings have diverse inclinations, the yogi’s faith may be directed toward any object whatsoever;
to demonstrate that even through meditation on such an object one achieves the desired success, he says:
"Or, from meditation on whatever is intended."
Commentary on Samādhi 39: When an object as intended—whether external, such as the moon, or internal, such as the network of channels (*nāḍicakra*)—is being cultivated, the mind becomes steady.

Having thus demonstrated the means, he speaks in order to show the result: "The mastery over this [meditative concentration] extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude; this is samādhi. (40)

Commentary: For the yogi who cultivates stability of the mind through these means, mastery—characterized by non-obstruction—arises by way of contemplating subtle objects, extending as far as the atom (*paramāṇu*). The meaning is that his mind is not obstructed anywhere, even in subtle objects down to the level of an atom. Likewise, for one who contemplates gross objects, from space up to the ultimate magnitude, no obstruction arises anywhere in the consciousness; the meaning is that there is complete sovereignty everywhere.
Thus, by means of these methods, he explains what the nature of the cultivated mind becomes:

"The meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of one whose mental fluctuations have ceased is the state of being established in and colored by that [object] with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable, like a noble gem."
Commentary on Samādhi 41:

He whose mental modifications (*vṛtti*) have ceased is one whose modifications are exhausted (*kṣīṇavṛtti*). For such a person, there occurs a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) characterized by "abiding in that" and "being colored by that" with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable—that is, the self, the senses, and their objects.
"Abiding in that" means one-pointedness upon those [objects].
The meaning is that "becoming like that" (tadañjanatā) is the state of being absorbed in that;
when the mind has become attenuated, there is an intensification of the very object being meditated upon,
such that an attainment of that kind occurs, which is a transformation into that very form.
He provides an illustration: "Like a noble gem.

Just as a noble, stainless crystal gem assumes various forms under the influence of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), so too the stainless mind assumes various forms through its coloring by the respective objects of meditation.

Although it was stated [earlier] that this occurs "among the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped," nevertheless, according to the sequence of the stages (*bhūmikā*), it should be understood as occurring "among the grasped, the grasping, and the grasper."

Since concentration first has the object of perception as its focus, then it has the act of perception as its focus, and then it takes the form of pure "I-am-ness" (asmitā) with the perceiver as its focus— because it is impossible for the solitary Puruṣa, the perceiver, to be an object of contemplation— the mind, colored by the gross and subtle objects of perception, becomes absorbed therein. In this way, it should be understood that the mind becomes absorbed in the act of perception and in the perceiver as well.
Now he describes the fourfold nature of that very attainment (samāpatti) just mentioned:
"The attainment mixed with conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, object, and knowledge is *savitarka*."
Commentary on Samādhi 42: Sound is that which is perceivable by the auditory faculty, either in the form of *sphoṭa* or as articulated speech;
the object [of cognition] consists of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth.
Knowledge is a modification of the intellect (buddhi) in which sattva predominates;
conceptualization has the definition previously stated;
[the objects] are mixed with these.

That meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) in which these three—sound and the others—appear in the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through mutual superimposition, in this manner: "the word is 'cow,' the object is 'cow,' the cognition is 'cow,'" is called *savitarka*.
[Sūtra 42] He now describes the *nirvitarka* (non-conceptual) state, which is the opposite of the characteristics just mentioned:
When memory is purified, the state of concentration (samādhi) in which the object alone appears as if devoid of its own nature is *nirvitarka* (non-discursive).

When the recollection of words and their meanings has dissolved, the attainment (*samāpatti*) is called *nirvitarka* because it manifests with the clear form of the perceived object appearing directly, while the aspect of cognition itself becomes subordinate, making it appear as if empty of its own nature.
In order to demonstrate another division, he says:
"By this very [same method], the subtle-objected [samādhis] with deliberation and without deliberation are explained."
Commentary on Samādhi 44: By this very [explanation of] attainment with vitarka and without vitarka, that with vicāra and without vicāra is also explained; of what nature is it?
"Subtle-objected" means that its object consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and so forth;
by this, it is established that the former [meditation] has gross objects,
for it takes the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) and the sense organs as its objective support.
That [samādhi] in which a subtle object appears—delimited by space, time, qualities, and so forth, and accompanied by conceptualizations of words and their meanings—is *savicārā*.

That in which a subtle object appears as the mere substrate (*dharmimātra*), devoid of space, time, qualities, and so forth, and taking the form of the *tanmātras* and the sense organs, is *nirvicārā*.

Regarding this very [meditation] which has a subtle object, he asks: what is the ultimate limit of the subtle object? He says: "And the state of having a subtle object culminates in the unmanifest (aliṅga)" (Sūtra 45).

Commentary: Regarding the statement that the subtle objectivity of the two types of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)—with deliberation (*savicāra*) and without deliberation (*nirvicāra*)—culminates in the unmanifest (*aliṅga*):
it does not dissolve anywhere, nor does it indicate or lead to anything else; thus, the *aliṅga* is the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*).
Subtle objectivity extends as far as that.

To explain: in the transformation of the *guṇas*, there are four stages—the specific mark (*viśiṣṭaliṅga*), the non-specific mark (*aviśiṣṭaliṅga*), the mere mark (*liṅgamātra*), and the markless (*aliṅga*).
The specific mark consists of the elements and the sense organs; the non-specific mark consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The intellect is characterized by having a mark (liṅga), whereas the Pradhāna is without a mark (aliṅga);
it is thereby stated that there exists nothing subtler than this.
Regarding these attainments (*samāpatti*), he states their purpose in the present context:
"These very [attainments] are the seeded concentration (*sabīja-samādhi*)."

Commentary on Sūtra 46: Those aforementioned attainments (*samāpatti*) are called "seeded" (*sabīja*) because they exist together with a seed—that is, with an objective support (*ālambana*). This is termed "cognitive" (*samprajñāta*) samādhi, since all of them possess an objective support.
Now, because the other attainments have non-discursive thought as their fruit, he states the fruit of the non-discursive [attainment]:
"From proficiency in non-discursive thought, there is internal clarity and samādhi. (47)
Commentary: "The state of being beyond reflection" has been explained [in sūtra 1.44].
"Clarity" means purity.
In comparison with that which possesses vitarka and has a gross object, that which is without vitarka is superior;
compared to that, too, is that which possesses vicāra and has a subtle object;
and compared to that, again, is that which is without vicāra.
When that non-conceptual state, through the power of intense practice, attains proficiency and purity, inner clarity (*adhyātmaprasāda*) arises;
the mind becomes free from the latent impressions of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) and fit for a continuous flow of stability.
This very firmness in stability is what constitutes the proficiency of the mind.
To the question "What happens when that exists?", he says:
"In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing."
Commentary on Samādhi 48:
It bears *ṛta* (the right) and truth, and is never obscured by error; that is the wisdom known as *ṛtambharā*. The meaning is that it arises in that [state].
And from that light of wisdom, seeing everything as it truly is, the yogin attains preeminent yoga.
He states its distinction from other types of wisdom:
"It has a different object than the wisdoms of hearing and inference, because it pertains to specific characteristics."
Commentary on Samādhi 49: "Learning" (*śruta*) is knowledge derived from scripture;
"inference" (*anumāna*) has the characteristics already described. (1)
7) The wisdom that arises from those two has a general object as its domain;
for words and logical marks lack the capacity to apprehend particulars, unlike the sense faculties.

Furthermore, this wisdom (*prajñā*), which arises from the confidence of being free from discursive investigation (*nirvicāra-vaiśāradya*), is distinct from those two [previous stages] because its object is specific.
For in this wisdom, even the particulars of things that are subtle, concealed, or remote appear in a perfectly clear form;
therefore, it is taught that the yogi must exert supreme effort toward this very [wisdom].
He states the fruit of this wisdom:
"The impression born from it obstructs other impressions."

Commentary on Sūtra 50: The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that wisdom obstructs other impressions—both those arising from the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) and those born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—meaning it renders them incapable of performing their own functions.

This is because the impressions generated by this [wisdom] through its nature as reality (*tattva*) are powerful, and thus they are able to sublate the impressions produced by wisdom whose nature is non-reality (*atattva*).
Therefore, it is implied that one should practice that very wisdom.
Having thus described *samprajñāta-samādhi*, he speaks in order to describe *asamprajñāta-samādhi*: [Yoga Sūtra 1.18]...
Upon the cessation of that [cognitive concentration] as well, because of the cessation of everything, there is seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*).

When even that cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta*) is ceased—that is, when it dissolves—because all mental modifications (*citta-vṛtti*) have dissolved back into their cause, a modification arises from mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra-mātra*). By means of the negation "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), which is a simple exclusion (*paryudāsa*), seedless concentration occurs; when this exists, the Person (*puruṣa*) becomes established in its own nature and pure.

51. The Bodhisattva’s practice of giving is inexhaustible because it is not based on a basis. Why? Because the bodhisattva does not perceive a basis. Furthermore, that which is the basis of giving is itself without basis; therefore, the bodhisattva’s practice of giving is inexhaustible. This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible practice of giving. What is the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible practice of morality? Here, the bodhisattva practices morality while not perceiving a basis. Why? Because the bodhisattva does not perceive a basis. Furthermore, that which is the basis of morality is itself without basis; therefore, the bodhisattva’s practice of morality is inexhaustible. Thus, in this [chapter], having stated the definition of the yoga under discussion; having explained the terms "cessation of mental fluctuations" (*cittavṛttinirodha*); having described the nature and divisions of the two means characterized by practice (*abhyāsa*) and detachment (*vairāgya*); having declared the primary and secondary divisions of yoga through the distinction between *samprajñāta* and *asamprajñāta*; having extensively demonstrated the means following an exposition of the practice of yoga; and having, with the aim of showing easy methods, determined the nature, proofs, powers, designations, and meditations (*upāsanā*) of Īśvara along with their fruits; having described the distractions of the mind (*cittavikṣepa*) and their concomitants such as pain (*duḥkha*) in detail, as well as the various means for their cessation—such as practice, friendliness (*maitrī*), and so forth, as well as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other techniques; having explained the cognitive activity directed toward objects which serves as a preliminary limb for both *samprajñāta* and *asamprajñāta*, along with its characteristics and results, together with its respective objects; and having concluded with a summary of *samprajñāta* and *asamprajñāta*, the seedless (*nirbīja*) samādhi preceded by the seeded (*sabīja*) samādhi has been declared. Thus, the Yoga-pāda is fully expounded.

The First Chapter: Samādhi-pāda, from the *Pātañjalavṛtti* titled *Rājamārtaṇḍa*, composed by Bhojadeva, the Lord of Dhāra. Thus ends the First Chapter: Samādhi-pāda. Now begins the Second Chapter: Sādhana-pāda.
May that Lord of the World, the Three-Eyed One, by whom those means for the attainment of supernatural powers difficult to reach were revealed, grant the fulfillment of our prayers.

Thus, having explained yoga with its means for one whose mind is concentrated in the first quarter, [the author] now states *kriyāyoga* in order to demonstrate the practice of its means so that even for one whose mind is distracted, yoga may attain stability preceded by the cultivation of those means: "Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute *kriyāyoga*; it is the means. (YS 2.1)
Commentary: Austerity (*tapas*) refers to practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* prescribed in other scriptures;
self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the recitation of mantras preceded by the *praṇava*;
and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the dedication of all actions to Him, the Supreme Teacher, without regard for their fruits.
These are called "kriyā-yoga" (the yoga of action).
To the question "For what purpose is it? he says:

The purpose of the cultivation of concentration is for the purpose of thinning the afflictions; this is the second function. The afflictions are those to be described hereafter; their "thinning" is the obstruction of their ability to perform their own functions.
Concentration (*samādhi*) has the characteristics already described.
Its cultivation is the repeated application [of the mind] to the object; that which has this as its meaning or purpose is so described.

This is what is meant: these practices, beginning with austerity (tapas), when cultivated, loosen the afflictions such as ignorance (avidyā) residing in the mind and thereby serve to assist meditative absorption (samādhi).
Therefore, it has been taught that a yogi must first be devoted to the performance of the rules of action-yoga (kriyāyoga).
It was stated that [this practice] is for the purpose of attenuating the afflictions (*kleśa*); regarding this, he asks what the afflictions are and says:
ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to live (*abhiniveśa*) are the afflictions.
Commentary on Sādhana 3: Ignorance and the others, whose definitions will be stated hereafter, are five;
when they produce the torment characterized by affliction, they become denoted by the term "kleśa" (afflictions).
For when these [afflictions] operate within the mind, they strengthen the transformation of qualities characterized by formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Although all [afflictions] possess an equal degree of defilement, he says the following in order to demonstrate the preeminence of ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is the root of them all:

Ignorance is the field for the subsequent [afflictions]—whether dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active. Regarding the means [of their cessation]: ignorance is delusion, that is to say, the conceit of self in what is not-self.

That [ignorance] is the field, the soil for the growth of the subsequent [afflictions], such as egoism and the rest, which are each fourfold according to the distinctions of dormant, attenuated, and so forth;

therefore, where ignorance—in the form of erroneous cognition—is weakened, there the emergence of the afflictions such as egoism is not observed, since their emergence is seen only when erroneous cognition exists. Thus, the status of ignorance as the root is firmly established.

Regarding the categories of "dormant," "attenuated," "interrupted," and "exalted": among those, the afflictions (*kleśa*) that reside in the ground of the mind and do not initiate their own activity due to the absence of an awakening cause are called "dormant" (*prasupta*).
For example, in the state of childhood, the afflictions exist in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), yet they are not manifested because of the absence of an auxiliary awakening cause.

Those [latent dispositions] are "feeble" when their capacity to produce their own effects has been weakened by the cultivation of their respective antidotes; they remain in the mind as mere residual impressions (*vāsanā*), unable to initiate their own effects without a vast collection of auxiliary conditions—as is the case for a yogin who has practiced.

Those are "interrupted" when they persist with their power overcome by some other powerful affliction (*kleśa*), such as attachment (*rāga*) during a state of aversion (*dveṣa*), or aversion during a state of attachment;
for these two, being mutually contradictory, cannot exist simultaneously.

Those [factors] are "exalted" which, having obtained the presence of their respective auxiliary conditions, bring about their own respective effects; for example, those that are always obstacles to yoga during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).

Although ignorance (*avidyā*) exists as the fundamental basis for each of these four types, it is perceived as being inherent to them; indeed, the intrinsic nature of the afflictions is never observed anywhere to exist independently of their connection with error (*viparyaya*).

Therefore, when ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists of false knowledge, is removed by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), these [impressions], being like burnt seeds, have no further germination anywhere;
thus it is certain that they have ignorance as their cause and are connected with ignorance.
Consequently, all of them are designated as "ignorance."
Since all afflictions cause the distraction of the mind, the yogi must first of all exert effort toward their eradication; thus,
he states the definition of ignorance (avidyā):

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self; this is its function as a means [to bondage]. "The appearance of that which is not in that" is the general definition of ignorance.
The specific differentiation of that very [ignorance] is as follows: the conceit of permanence regarding impermanent things such as jars is called ignorance;
likewise, the conceit of purity regarding impure things such as the body; the conceit of happiness regarding painful sense-objects; and the conceit of selfhood regarding the non-self body.
By this, the delusion of merit regarding demerit and the delusion of benefit regarding harm are explained.
To define *asmitā*, he says: "The identity, as it were, of the power of the seer and the power of the seeing is *asmitā*."
Commentary on Sādhana 6: The Puruṣa is the power of seeing;
the sattvic transformation, which is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and is not overwhelmed by rajas and tamas, is the power of seeing.
The identification of these two—which are absolutely distinct in nature as enjoyer and enjoyed, and as conscious and unconscious—is called *asmitā* (I-am-ness).
Just as *prakṛti*, though in reality devoid of agency and enjoyment, conceives the notion "I am the agent," this is the affliction known as the misconception (*viparyāsa*) of *asmitā*.
He states the definition of attachment:
"Attachment is that which lies latent within pleasure.
(Sādhana 7)
Commentary: That which lies latent in pleasure is "latent in pleasure" (*sukhānuśayī*).

It is the affliction known as passion (*rāga*), characterized by greed, which takes the form of thirst for the means of pleasure and is preceded by the experience of pleasure in one who knows pleasure.
He states the definition of hatred:
Hatred is that which lies latent within suffering; this is the proof (sādhana). 8.
Commentary: Suffering has been defined previously.

For one who knows that [suffering], preceded by the recollection thereof, there arises a reviling anger toward its causes because of a lack of desire for them; this is the affliction characterized as hatred (dveṣa).
He states the characteristic of clinging (abhiniveśa): "Clinging is that which flows spontaneously and is so firmly rooted even in the wise" (Sādhana 9).

Commentary: Arising from the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of experiencing the pain of death in previous births, taking the form of fear, and manifesting as a continuous attachment day after day in the form of the thought "May I not be separated from my body, objects, and so forth," this affliction (*kleśa*) known as *abhiniveśa* (clinging to life) operates spontaneously in all beings, from the lowest worm up to Brahmā, even without an external cause.

Thus, since the state of ordinary waking activity (*vyutthāna*) consists essentially of these afflictions, those who desire to practice one-pointed concentration (*ekāgratā*) must first eliminate the afflictions.

Since it is not possible to effect their abandonment without knowing them, he has stated their enumeration, definition, field, and classification for the sake of that knowledge; and now, he explains the analysis of the means for abandoning them, which are divided into gross and subtle types:
"The subtle ones are to be abandoned by re-absorption" (sādhana 10).

Commentary: Those subtle afflictions which exist merely in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and do not initiate a transformation into their own active state are to be abandoned—that is, relinquished—by means of *pratiprasava*, which is retrogressive transformation. When the mind, having accomplished its purpose along with its latent impressions, has entered back into its own cause, *asmitā* (the sense of "I-am-ness"), then how can there be the possibility of those [afflictions] which have been uprooted?
He states the means for abandoning the gross [afflictions]: "Their fluctuations are to be abandoned by meditation."
Sādhana 11:

Commentary—The modifications (*vṛtti*) consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion belonging to those afflictions (*kleśa*) that have already begun to produce their effects are to be abandoned by meditation;
the meaning is that they are to be relinquished by means of meditation alone, characterized by one-pointedness of mind.
By the mere practice of purifying the mind, those [impurities] cease because they are gross; just as gross dirt on clothing and the like is removed by washing alone,
whereas the subtle portion remaining therein can only be removed by various means such as heating and so forth.

Having thus stated the true nature of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he speaks in order to state that of the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*): "The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions; it is to be experienced in the present life or in future lives."
Sādhana 12, Commentary: By the term "karmāśaya" (the storehouse of karma), its essential nature has been stated;
therefore, karmas are indeed of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

By the phrase "root of the afflictions" (kleśamūla), the cause is stated, since the afflictions alone are the motive for actions that are wholesome or unwholesome. By the phrase "to be experienced in seen and unseen births," the result is described: that which is to be experienced in this very life is "to be experienced in a seen birth."
That which is to be experienced in another birth is "to be experienced in a future life" (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*).

For instance, certain meritorious acts such as the propitiation of deities, when performed with intense spiritual fervor (*tīvrasaṃvega*), yield their fruit—characterized by [a specific] birth, lifespan, and experience—in this very life. Just as in the case of Nandīśvara, through the power of propitiating the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, distinguished birth and other qualities manifested in this very life;
likewise, in the cases of others such as Viśvāmitra and so forth, birth and lifespan [were attained] through the power of austerity (*tapas*).
For some, it is simply birth—as in the case of Nahuṣa and others who, having committed evil deeds with intense agitation, underwent a transformation into another species;
and as in the case of Urvaśī, who took the form of a creeper in the grove of Kārttikeya.
Thus, this should be applied appropriately, either individually or collectively, as the case may require.
Now he states the fruit of the latent deposit of karma (karmāśaya), distinguished by its own subdivisions:
"When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience."
Sādhana 13:
Commentary—The afflictions (*kleśa*) have the characteristics previously described;

while these remain unsubdued, there occurs the ripening (*vipāka*), that is, the fruit consisting of birth, lifespan, and experience, of actions (*karman*) in the form of wholesome and unwholesome states.
Birth (*jāti*) refers to being human and so forth;
lifespan (*āyus*) is the connection with a single body for a long period of time;

enjoyments (*bhoga*) are objects, the sense organs, and the cognitions of pleasure and pain—that is, pleasure, pain, and the like—since the word "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is derived through the understanding of its etymological components as "the experiencing of the state of action and instruments."

This is the intended meaning here: as the karmic impressions (vāsanās) accumulated on the ground of the mind since beginningless time reach maturity in various ways, they—existing in a relationship of primary and secondary factors—initiate their own effects, characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience.

He now states that birth and the other factors, which have been described as the fruits of karma and which follow their own causal karma, possess the agency of performing their respective effects: [13]
Those [actions] have joy and suffering as their fruits because they have merit and demerit as their causes.
Regarding the commentary on the means (sādhana): "joy" is happiness (*sukha*) and "suffering" is pain (*duḥkha*); those whose fruits are these two are described as such.
Merit (*puṇya*) is wholesome action (*kuśala-karma*), and its opposite is demerit (*apuṇya*); those for whom these two actions are the cause—of them, it is this that is meant:
birth, lifespan, and enjoyments originated from meritorious action have the fruit of pleasure, whereas those originated from non-meritorious action have the fruit of suffering.
And this twofold division is made with respect to all living beings.

Regarding the yogi, he says that all of it is suffering: "To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the fluctuations of the guṇas."

Commentary on Sādhana 15: For the discerning person (*vivekin*), who has fully understood the distinction [between the Self and the *kleśas*] and so forth, the entirety of the visible world (*dṛśyamātra*)—which is the means for all experience—is like sweet food mixed with poison; it is nothing but suffering, meaning it is to be experienced as entirely disagreeable.
This is because the yogi, being of such supreme refinement, is repelled even by a mere fragment of suffering.

Just as the eyeball experiences great pain from the mere touch of a woolen thread while other parts of the body do not, so too does the person of discrimination (vivekin) tremble at even a slight connection with suffering. To explain how this is so, he says: "By the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions. Regarding objects being enjoyed, because greed increases according to their nature, and because the pleasure and pain caused by the failure to obtain them cannot be avoided, they serve as the means for further suffering; thus, they possess no form of happiness whatsoever—this is the state of suffering through transformation (*pariṇāma-duḥkhatva*).

Since aversion toward the obstacles to the means of happiness is always present even while those means are being grasped, the suffering of pain (*tāpa-duḥkha*) is difficult to avoid even at the time of experiencing pleasure; thus, there is the nature of suffering as pain.

As for the suffering of mental formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), when objects both desired and undesired are encountered, the arising of cognitions of pleasure and cognitions of pain likewise initiates corresponding mental formations within their own field (*svakṣetra*).

From these formations, there again arises the experience of such cognitions; thus, because everything is permeated by suffering through the gateway of the production of immeasurable formations, it possesses the nature of suffering.
This is what is meant: because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and their fruition (*vipāka*) are not severed, everything is indeed suffering;
and furthermore, because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*.
For the functions of the *guṇas*—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which take the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion, arise in mutual opposition through the relationship of the overcome and the overcomer.
Because all of these are permeated by suffering in every respect, they possess the nature of suffering.

This is what is meant: for the discerning person who desires an absolute and final cessation of suffering and who possesses the aforementioned fourfold cause, all objects appear in the form of suffering;
therefore, it is stated that the ripening of all karma is indeed of the nature of suffering.

Thus, since this aforementioned mass of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and the accumulation of their results (*vipāka*) originates from ignorance (*avidyā*), and since ignorance—being of the nature of false knowledge—is to be destroyed by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and since right knowledge consists in the ascertainment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted along with its means, [the author] states that [ascertainment]:
"That which is to be abandoned is future suffering."
Commentary on Sādhana 16: Since what has already occurred is past and what is being experienced cannot be abandoned, it is stated that only future suffering of saṃsāra is to be relinquished.
He states the cause of that which is to be abandoned:
"The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned; this is the means. (Sādhana 17)
Commentary: The seer is the Puruṣa whose nature is consciousness; the seen is the intellect-substance (buddhi-sattva).

That conjunction of these two—which is preceded by the non-discrimination between them and consists in their proximity as enjoyer and enjoyed—is the cause, the reason, for the world-process (saṃsāra) which is the transformation of the Guṇas and is of the nature of suffering that is to be abandoned.
The meaning is that through the cessation of that [ignorance], the cessation of saṃsāra occurs;
thus it was stated that there is a conjunction between the seer and the seen.

In this regard, he states the nature, the function, and the purpose of the object of perception: "The object of perception (dṛśya) consists of the elements and the sense organs, its nature being illumination, activity, and inertia; it exists for the sake of experience and liberation" (Sādhana 18).
Commentary: Illumination is the attribute of *sattva*;
activity, in the form of engagement, is that of *rajas*;
and stability, in the form of restraint, is that of *tamas*.

That whose nature consists of manifestation (*prakāśa*), activity (*kriyā*), and stability (*sthiti*), and whose inherent form (*svābhāvikaṃ rūpam*) is such, is thus described as its essential character (*svarūpam*).

"Consisting of the elements and the senses" (*bhūtendriyātmakam*) means that the elements (*bhūtāni*) are of two kinds— distinguished as gross and subtle— namely, earth and the others, as well as the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) of smell and the rest.
The senses are threefold, distinguished as the organs of cognition, the organs of action, and the internal organ.
Both of these constitute its object; that whose transformation is non-different from its own nature consists of this very form of the grasped and the grasper—by this, its function is stated.
Experience is as previously defined.
Apavarga is the cessation of transmigratory existence preceded by discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti).
The meaning is that the "visible" (dṛśya) is that which has those two—enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga)—as its purpose (prayojana).
Since that which is perceptible— which consists of the transformation of various states and forms— must be known as something to be abandoned, he speaks in order to describe its states:
"The stages of the guṇas are the specific, the non-specific, the mere indicative, and the unindicative" (Sādhana 19).
Commentary: It has been taught that four stages (parvan), which are specific states of the guṇas, are to be known.

Among these, the "specifics" (viśeṣa) are the gross elements (mahābhūta) and the sense organs (indriya); the "non-specifics" (aviśeṣa) are the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
It has been stated that the intellect (*buddhi*) is "possessing a mark" (*liṅgamātra*), while the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is "without a mark" (*aliṅga*).

Because the unmanifest, whose nature consists of the three *guṇas*, is recognized as persisting through everything by way of its underlying continuity, it must necessarily be known; therefore, four stages (*parva*) have been specified for the time of yoga.

Thus, because the object of perception (dṛśya) must first be known as that which is to be abandoned, [the Sūtra] has explained it along with its states; now, in order to explain the subject of perception (draṣṭṛ), who is that which is to be accepted, it says: "The seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he beholds the mental modifications."
