Commentary on Sādhana 20: The seer is the *puruṣa*, consisting of pure seeing (*dṛśimātra*), which is mere consciousness (*cetanāmātra*).
The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding both attributes (*dharma*) and the substratum of attributes (*dharmī*).
For some indeed maintain that volition is a quality of the Self;
though it is pure, because it lacks the nature of transformation and so forth, it is self-established, yet it observes the conditions.
"Conditions" refers to the consciousnesses colored by objects; it observes them directly, without interval, and without any process of transition.
This is what is meant: the Puruṣa’s status as a seer (draṣṭṛ) occurs solely by its mere proximity to the intellect (buddhi) when that intellect is colored by an object;
he states that this very [Puruṣa] is the enjoyer (bhoktṛ).
The very purpose of the object of perception is its own nature;

this is the meaning of the function [of the means]. That is to say, the "self" (ātman) of the object of perception—that which has the characteristics previously described—is its very essence (svarūpa), and it is for that purpose alone [that the means operate].
Its purpose, namely the accomplishment of the Spirit's state as an enjoyer of the objects of human life, consists in the relinquishing of its own purpose;
for the Pradhāna, when it proceeds, does not proceed with any purpose of its own, but rather in order to accomplish the Spirit's state as an enjoyer.

If, in this way, the sole purpose of the Puruṣa were merely the accomplishment of experience, then once that [experience] has been accomplished, the [Prakṛti] would become purposeless and cease its activity.

Furthermore, when it is devoid of transformation, all perceivers (draṣṭṛ) would be liberated due to its purity, and consequently, there would be the cessation of saṃsāra. Anticipating this objection, he says:

With respect to one who has achieved their purpose (*kṛtārtha*), [the *guṇas*] are destroyed, yet they are not destroyed because they are common to others; this is the function of the means (*sādhana*).

— Although, by producing experience up until the point of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), they have ceased their activity with respect to some individual person who has achieved their purpose and are thus "destroyed" for them, nevertheless, because they are common to all persons, they remain with their activity undestroyed with respect to others.
Therefore, because the Pradhāna is common to all enjoyers, it can never be destroyed;
nor does the liberation of one individual entail the liberation of all—this is what has been stated.

Having explained the seen and the seer, he speaks in order to explain their conjunction: "Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the essential natures of the power of the master and the power of the owned; it is the means. (Sādhana 23)
Commentary: He defines this [the object] by way of its function:
the power of the object is the nature of the perceivable, while the power of the subject is the essential form of the seer.
The conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is that which is the cause of the perception of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of both of those two— which are established as the object of cognition and the cognizer—
and it is innate (*sahaja*), being non-different from the very nature of the relationship between the enjoyed and the enjoyer;
for there is no conjunction whatsoever distinct from the essential nature of those two, who are eternal and all-pervading.

That very state of being an object of enjoyment belonging to the enjoyer and the state of being an enjoyer belonging to the object of enjoyment, established from time immemorial, is itself conjunction (saṃyoga).
He states the cause of that as well:
Its cause is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is its means (*sādhana*)—
that ignorance, consisting of perversion and having the nature of delusion (*moha*), which was previously explained (2).
4–5) That [ignorance] is the cause of that conjunction which consists of non-discriminative cognition (avivekakhyāti).
That which is to be abandoned is said to be the object of the act of abandoning.
What, then, is that "abandonment"? He says: "In the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of conjunction; this abandonment is the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the seer.
(Sūtra 2.25)

Commentary: When that ignorance has been uprooted by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), which is diametrically opposed to its own nature, there occurs its non-existence; when that [non-existence] exists, there is also the non-existence of its effect, namely *saṃyoga* (conjunction), and this is called "its abandonment" (*taddhāna*).

The meaning is this: a spatial division of this formless entity is not possible; rather, once discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen, the conjunction caused by non-discrimination ceases of its own accord—this is its abandonment. And that very abandonment of conjunction is designated as the eternal isolation (*kaivalya*) of the eternally isolated *puruṣa*.
Thus, the nature, cause, and effect of the conjunction with the visible have been explained.
Now, by means of stating the method for its abandonment, he describes the cause for that which is to be adopted:
Unshakable discriminative discernment is the means for liberation;
this is the second sūtra.

Commentary: The discernment—that the gunas are one thing and the Puruṣa is another—such a discernment, its manifestation or clear knowledge, is the means, that is, the cause, for this liberation, which is the relinquishing of the visible world of suffering.
What is "uninterrupted" (*aviplavā*)? It is that in which no interruption—that is, a break characterized by rising again at intervals—exists; such is the uninterrupted [practice].

The intended meaning here is this: when ignorance has been dissolved through the power of cultivating the counter-measures, there occurs a transfer of the reflection of consciousness into the intellect (*buddhi*), which has turned inward and is no longer overwhelmed by the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, and in which the conceit of being an agent or an enjoyer has ceased; this is called discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*).
And when that [cognitive process] has proceeded as a continuous stream, isolation (*kaivalya*) indeed occurs through the cessation of the authority of the object-of-sight (26).
Describing the nature of the wisdom (*prajñā*) that arises for a person who has attained discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), he states the very essence of that discernment:
His wisdom has sevenfold application in the final stage (sādhana 27,

vṛtti): the meaning is that for one who has produced discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*), the wisdom consisting of the discrimination of what is to be known becomes sevenfold in the final stage, at the limit of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) that possess an object of focus (*sālambana*).
In that regard, liberation from activity consists of four types.
Thus, when such sevenfold wisdom of the stages has arisen, a person is called "isolated.
It has been stated that discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the cause for the cessation of the conjunction [of the seer and the seen].
Now, he explains what the instrumental cause is for its arising:
"From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to discriminative discernment."
Commentary on Sādhana 28: The limbs of yoga (yogāṅga) will be described hereafter.

From their performance—that is, from practice preceded by knowledge—comes the destruction of impurity (*aśuddhi*). When the impurity of the *sattva* of the mind, which consists of afflictions (*kleśa*) that are forms of obscuration to its luminosity, is destroyed, there arises an illumination of knowledge. This is a *sāttvika* transformation that proceeds through various degrees until it culminates in discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). The meaning is that [the limbs of yoga] are the cause of that discernment.
It has been stated that the destruction of impurity results from the practice of the limbs of yoga;
what, then, are those limbs of yoga? He provides their enumeration as follows:

The eight limbs—yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi—are the means (sādhana). Commentary: Among these, some are direct auxiliaries to samādhi, such as dhāraṇā and the others; others assist samādhi by way of uprooting contrary thoughts such as violence, namely yama and the rest.
In this context, each subsequent factor serves as an aid to the preceding one; for example, when mastery of posture (*āsana*) is attained, there is stability in breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
and the same principle should be applied to the subsequent stages as well.
He states their essential nature in sequence:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*.
Commentary on Sādhana 30: In this context, violence (*hiṃsā*) is indeed an activity whose purpose is the separation from life-force (*prāṇa*);
and it is the cause of all misfortune.

Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is indeed the absence of that [violence], because violence must be avoided in every possible way; therefore, non-violence, which consists in the absence of that, is mentioned first.
Truthfulness (*satya*) is the correspondence of speech and mind with reality.
Theft is the taking away of another's property; its absence is non-stealing. Celibacy is restraint of the generative organ.
Non-possessiveness is the refusal to accept the means of enjoyment.
These five, beginning with non-violence, are designated by the term *yama* and are taught as limbs of yoga (30).
He states their specific distinctions:
Unrestricted by caste, place, time, or occasion, and universal in scope, this is the Great Vow (mahāvrata).
[Sādhanapāda 31] Commentary: Caste refers to being a Brahmin and so forth.
The place is a sacred site and so forth;
the time is the fourteenth day and so forth; the occasion is the purpose of the Brahmins and so forth.

The previously mentioned restraints (*yama*), such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest, when practiced without these four types of limitations across all stages of the mind—beginning with the "distracted" (*kṣipta*) and so forth—are called the "Great Vow" (*mahāvrata*).

For example: "I shall not kill a Brāhmaṇa," "I shall not kill anyone at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*)," "I shall not kill on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight," or "I shall not kill anyone except for the sake of the gods or Brāhmaṇas. In this way, they are "unlimited" (*anavacchinna*) when one resolves: "I shall not kill anything, at any time, for any purpose whatsoever," being free from the aforementioned fourfold limitations.

In this way, [the term] should be applied as appropriate to the "truths" (satya) and so forth; thus, when these are practiced in an unrestricted manner according to the general rule, they are called the "Great Vow" (mahāvrata), and not through the restrictive limitation of another's specific definition.
He states the observances:
"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances; they are the means. (Yoga Sūtra 2.32)
Commentary: Purity is twofold—external and internal.

External purity is the cleansing of the body and so forth with earth, water, and the like; internal purity is the cleansing of the impurities of the mind through loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
Contentment is satisfaction;
the remaining [virtues] have already been explained previously.
These [practices], beginning with purity (śauca), are denoted by the term "observances" (niyama).
To the question, "In what way do these constitute limbs of yoga? he says:

The cultivation of the counteragent for the obstruction of discursive thoughts is the means [of accomplishment]. Commentary: Discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) are so called because they are thought over; they are indeed obstacles to yoga, such as violence and the like.

When there is the cultivation of their counter-measures, if an obstruction arises, then yoga becomes easy to accomplish; thus, the status of the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama) as limbs of yoga is indeed established.
Now, he describes the nature, the varieties of divisions, and the results of the discursive thoughts (vitarka) in sequence:

Reflection on the counter-measures (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*) consists in understanding that mental deliberations (*vitarka*) such as violence and so forth—whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; and whether mild, moderate, or intense—result in infinite fruits of suffering and ignorance.
(Sādhana 34). Commentary: These aforementioned [faults] such as violence are first divided into three types according to the distinctions of being performed, caused to be performed, or approved.

In this context, "done" (*kṛta*) refers to those actions performed by oneself; "caused to be done" (*kārita*) refers to those produced through the activity of an instigator, such as saying "do it"; and "approved" (*anumodita*) refers to those being performed by another which are accepted with approval, such as saying "well done."
And this threefold classification is stated for the purpose of mutual clarification and definitive determination;
otherwise, one of dull intellect might think, "Since the injury was not committed by me personally, I am without fault.
It is therefore said that these [actions] are preceded by greed, anger, and delusion, in order to demonstrate their causes.

Although greed (*lobha*) was mentioned first, nevertheless, because delusion (*moha*)—characterized by the conceit of self in what is not-self—is the root cause of all afflictions, one should understand its status as the fundamental basis; for when that [delusion] exists, greed, anger, and the rest arise preceded by the distinction between self and other. The meaning is that every category of fault is preceded by delusion. Greed is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Anger (*krodha*) is a mental state characterized by combustion that uproots the discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

Although each [of the three], such as violence and the rest, is of three kinds according to the distinctions of being committed and so forth, they are further divided into three types based on their causes, such as delusion (*moha*).
He states again their threefold nature according to the distinction of their degrees: mild, moderate, and intense (*mṛdu-madhya-adhimātra*).
The mild are dull, neither sharp nor medium;
the medium are neither dull nor sharp;
the superior are sharp.
The latter nine types thus constitute three categories, making twenty-seven in total;
for even among the "weak" and the others, each can further be divided into three— weak, medium, and intense.
It should be applied according to the appropriate correspondence, as follows:
weak-weak, weak-medium, and weak-intense.

Regarding their fruit, he says: they have the endless fruits of suffering and ignorance; suffering is a quality of the mind belonging to the *rajas* [quality], which appears as something disagreeable.

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) consists of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) in the form of doubt and error; those [afflictions] for which suffering and ignorance are the endless and unlimited fruits are so described.

Thus, it is taught that once these [afflictions] have been understood through their distinctions of essential nature, cause, and so forth, the yogi must effect their abandonment by means of the cultivation of their opposites (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*).
To explain in sequence how the spontaneously arising perfections (*siddhis*) come about as these [virtues] reach excellence through the power of practice, he says:
"When non-violence is firmly established, hostility ceases in his presence."
Commentary on Sādhana 35:
For one who cultivates non-violence (ahiṃsā), even those creatures such as snakes and mongooses that are natural enemies abandon their hostility in his presence and remain free from enmity;
the meaning is that even those of a violent nature renounce violence.
He states what occurs for one who practices truth:
"When there is firm establishment in truth, there is the state of being the locus of the fruits of action."
Commentary on Sādhana 36: For sacrificial acts and the like, when being performed, bestow fruits such as heaven;
however, for that yogin who possesses the practice of truth, truth is so perfected that the yogin attains the fruit even without performing the ritual action.
The meaning is that by his word, the fruit of the action accrues even to someone who does not perform the action themselves.
(36) He states the fruit for one who practices non-stealing:

When non-stealing is firmly established, there is the manifestation of all jewels; this is the commentary on verse 37: when one practices non-stealing, then through its excellence, divine jewels manifest from all sides even for one who is free from desire.
He states the fruit of the practice of celibacy: when celibacy is firmly established, there is the attainment of vigor.
Commentary on Sādhana 38: Indeed, for one who practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*), through its excellence, an unsurpassed vigor (*vīrya*) or capacity manifests;
for when celibacy reaches its peak, vigor attains excellence within the body, the senses, and the mind.
He states the fruit of non-possessiveness:
"When non-possessiveness is firmly established, there is thorough knowledge of 'how' and 'why' regarding birth."
The commentary on Sādhana 39: The state of "how" is *kathantā*; the "how" regarding birth is *janmakathantā*.

The awakening to that [ignorance] is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). The meaning is that when there is the desire to know—"Who was I in another birth? Of what nature was I? What actions did I perform?"—one knows everything correctly.
Not only is the acquisition of the means of enjoyment considered "possession" (*parigraha*), but even the acquisition of one's own body is possession, because the body is a means of enjoyment.
As long as that [body] exists, due to the persistence of attachment, activity remains only extroverted, and thus the manifestation of ultimate knowledge does not occur.

Furthermore, when one adopts equanimity without dependence on the acquisition of a body and so forth, then for that neutral person, through the abandonment of passion and the like, the comprehension of previous and subsequent births certainly becomes a cause for right knowledge. (39) Thus have been described the perfections of the restraints (*yama*).
Now he states the observances (niyamas): "From purity comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others; this is the means. 40

Commentary: For one who cultivates purity, a sense of disgust and loathing arises even toward one's own limbs by way of reflecting upon their causal nature—that is, "This body is impure; no attachment should be placed herein.

For this very reason, there is non-association with others who possess bodies, meaning an absence of contact or the avoidance of association. Indeed, how could one who feels disgust for his own body because he perceives its various defects enter into association with the similarly defective bodies of others?
He states another result of purity itself: "Purification of the mind, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self."
Sādhana 41, Commentary: The words "they come to be" complete the sentence.
*Sattva* consists of luminosity, pleasure, and so forth; its purity (*śuddhi*) is its non-overpowering by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Joy (*saumanasya*) is mental delight resulting from the absence of weariness;
one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) is the stability of the mind upon a fixed object;
and mastery over the senses (*indriyajaya*) is the abiding of the senses, which have turned away from their objects, within the self.

The fitness or capability of the mind for the vision of the Self, which consists of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), arises only for one who practices purity; these qualities, beginning with the purification of *sattva*, manifest in succession.
For instance, from the purification of *sattva* comes cheerfulness (*saumanasyam*).
From mental gladness comes one-pointedness;
from one-pointedness comes mastery over the senses;
from that, fitness for the vision of the self.
He states the fruit of the practice of contentment: "From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness."
Sādhana 42, Commentary: Through the excellence of contentment, such internal bliss arises for the yogi that even a hundredth part of external sensual pleasure cannot equal.
He states the fruit of austerity: "The perfection of the body and the senses results from the destruction of impurities through austerity; this is the means. (43)

Commentary: Asceticism (tapas), when practiced intensely, bestows a high degree of perfection upon the body and the senses by means of the destruction of the impurities of the mind, such as the afflictions (kleśa).

This is the meaning: through the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such practices, the afflictions of the mind are destroyed; from that destruction, the capacity of the senses and so forth to perceive the subtle, the concealed, and the remote becomes manifest, and the body attains qualities such as atomicity and magnitude at will.
He states the fruit of the study of one's own Vedic texts (svādhyāya): "From the study of one's own Vedic texts comes communion with the chosen deity" (Sūtra 4.1.44).
Commentary: When one's self-study (*svādhyāya*), characterized by the recitation of intended mantras and so forth, is being perfected, there occurs a union with the desired deity;
that is to say, the deity becomes directly perceptible.
He states the fruit of devotion to the Lord:
"Perfection in samādhi results from devotion to the Lord" (Sūtra 45).

Commentary: From that specific devotion which is the focused application (*praṇidhāna*) toward the Lord (*īśvara*), there occurs the manifestation of *samādhi* as previously defined; for when that Blessed Lord, the *īśvara*, is pleased, He removes the afflictions (*kleśa*) that constitute obstacles and brings about the awakening of *samādhi*.
(45) Having described the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), he states the posture (*āsana*).

Posture (āsana) is that which is firm and pleasant; its practice consists of the lotus posture (padmāsana), the staff posture (daṇḍāsana), the cross-legged posture (svastikāsana), and so forth. (Sūtra 46) Commentary: It is called *āsana* because one sits (*āsya*) upon it. It includes the lotus posture, the staff posture, the cross-legged posture, and others.
When that [mind] becomes steady, unwavering, blissful, and free from agitation, then it attains the status of being a limb of yoga (yogāṅga).
To explain the means for attaining that very steadiness and bliss, he says:

The means [of achieving steadiness] is through relaxation of effort and meditative absorption on infinity. (YS 1.36) — The connection is that that posture becomes steady and comfortable through relaxation of effort and through meditative absorption on infinity.
Whenever one forms the desire, "I shall assume the posture," then and there the posture is accomplished without even the slightest effort due to the relaxation of exertion.

Furthermore, when the mind attains meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) upon infinity, such as that of space, and through focused attention reaches identity with it, then, because of the absence of the ego-sense of the body (*dehāhaṃkāra*), the posture does not become a source of pain.
And when this mastery of posture is achieved, obstacles to concentration (*samādhi*), such as bodily tremors and the like, no longer prevail.
He states the fruit that arises as a consequence of that very [practice]:
"From that, there is no affliction by the pairs of opposites."

Sādhana 48, commentary: The meaning is that when mastery over the postures has been achieved, the yogi is not afflicted by the pairs of opposites, such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and so forth.
Immediately after the mastery of posture, he describes breath control (prāṇāyāma):
"When that [posture] is present, the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is breath control; this is the means. (YS 2.49)
Commentary: When stability of posture has been attained, a specific limb of yoga characterized by breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is caused by that [stability], becomes to be practiced.
Of what nature is it?
It is characterized by the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation.

Inhalation and exhalation have been defined [in the previous sūtra]. Their suspension—the interruption of the flow of movement through the three modes of exhaling, retaining, and filling, within the external and internal locations—is called *prāṇāyāma*.
To facilitate its easy comprehension, he explains its essential nature by dividing it:
"That [prāṇāyāma], however, which functions externally, internally, and as a suspension [of breath], is observed in terms of place, time, and number; it is long and subtle" (Sūtra 50).
Commentary: External activity is inhalation (recaka);
internal activity is exhalation (pūraka);
and internal stationary activity is breath-retention (kumbhaka).

In that [state], the vital breaths are established in immobility like water in a jar; thus it is called *kumbhaka*. This threefold *prāṇāyāma* becomes known as "long" (*dīrgha*) and "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) when characterized by place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), and number (*saṃkhyā*). Characterized by place, for example, from the nose to the *dvādaśānta*; the meaning is: starting from the nose up to a distance of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅguli*).

It is characterized by time, such as having a measure of thirty-six *mātrās* and so forth; it is characterized by number, such as "this many times performed" or "by this many inhalations and exhalations the first *udghāta* occurs"—
the grasping of number is employed for the sake of this knowledge.
"Udghāta" (upward strike) is the striking of the air, impelled from the base of the navel, against the head.
Having described three types of *prāṇāyāma*, he speaks in order to describe the fourth: [50]

The fourth means of practice (sādhana) is that which projects the external and internal objects; this is the function (vṛtti). The external object of the vital breath (prāṇa) consists of the nose, the dvādaśānta, and so forth.
The internal object consists of the heart, the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), and so forth.
Having directed [the breath] toward these two objects—that is, having reflected upon them—the suspension of movement that takes the form of a pillar is the fourth *prāṇāyāma*.

This is its distinction from the third, which is called *kumbhaka*: the latter is accomplished by a simultaneous state of suspension, without reflecting on the external or internal objects, according to the analogy of water falling suddenly onto a heated stone.
But this cessation, which subsumes two objects,
should also be understood, as before, to be characterized by place, time, and number. 51
He states the fruit of these fourfold [practices]:
"Thereupon, the veil over the light is destroyed" (Sādhana 52).

Commentary: Therefore, from that breath control (prāṇāyāma), the obscuration consisting of the afflictions (kleśa) which belongs to the luminosity residing in the *sattva* of the mind (*citta*) is diminished; that is to say, it perishes.
(52) He states another result:
The mental state conducive to the *dhāraṇās* is the means [of practice].

(53) The commentary: *Dhāraṇās* are those whose characteristics will be described later; when the mind, its defects diminished by *prāṇāyāmas*, is fixed upon whatever object, it becomes steady there and does not fall into distraction.
He states the definition of withdrawal (pratyāhāra):
"Withdrawal is as it were the imitation by the senses of the nature of the mind when they are not in contact with their own objects."
Sādhana 54:

Commentary—Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is that in which the senses are drawn back from their objects. As to how this is accomplished, he says: for the senses, such as the eye and so forth, "contact with their own objects" means functioning by being directed toward form and the like; the "absence of that" means remaining in their own essential nature alone, having abandoned that outward orientation.

When that [mind] exists, the senses become followers of the mind alone; since all the senses are observed to follow the mind just as bees follow the king bee, they are withdrawn when the mind is restrained. This imitation of its own nature by them is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
54. He states the fruit of withdrawal (pratyāhāra):
"Thereafter, there is supreme mastery over the senses."
Commentary on Sādhana 55:
For when withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is practiced, the senses become so subdued and brought under control that they do not go even when being led toward external objects; such is the meaning.

Thus, having described the *kriyā-yoga*—which has the fruit of attenuating the afflictions (*kleśa*) that constitute limbs of the yoga characterized by the first quarter [of the Yoga Sūtras]—and having stated the enumeration, nature, cause, field, and fruit of the afflictions; and having further stated the division, cause, nature, and fruit of actions (*karman*); the cause and nature of maturation (*vipāka*) have also been explained.

Therefore, because the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth are to be abandoned, and because their abandonment is impossible without knowledge (*jñāna*), and because knowledge depends upon the scripture (*śāstra*), and because the scripture possesses a fourfold structure (*caturvyūha*) by way of making known that which is to be avoided and the cause of its avoidance, as well as that which is to be adopted and the cause of its adoption; and because the essential nature of that which is to be avoided cannot be established apart from its avoidance—having thus described the fourfold structure together with its avoidance and accompanied by its respective causes; and having explained the nature and results of the restraints (*yama*) and so forth, which serve as the causes for discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*)—the cause for that which is to be adopted—and which exist in the relationship of internal and external factors; and having stated the enumeration of the postures (*āsana*) and so forth, ending with concentration (*dhāraṇā*), which stand in a mutual relationship of helper and helped; the definition and result of each has been declared.

Thus, this yoga—having attained the state of a seed through the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), having sprouted through postures (*āsana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and having flowered through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*)—will bear fruit through meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*); thus has the *Sādhanapāda* been explained. This concludes the *Sādhanapāda*, the second book, in the commentary on the *Pātañjala-yoga* entitled *Rājamārtaṇḍa*, composed by Bhoja, the Lord of Dhārā. [End of Sādhanapāda 2] Vibhūtipāda (The Book on Supernatural Powers)
Now begins the third chapter, the Vibhūtipāda (The Chapter on Supernatural Powers),
by the remembrance of whose lotus feet the supernatural powers such as aṇimā and others arise.

May that Lord of Beings be for the welfare of those who seek existence. Thus, having first designated the three limbs beginning with *dhāraṇā*, he begins to define them in order to establish the external, internal, and other types of accomplishments, by means of the technical term *saṃyama*. Among these, he states the essential nature of *dhāraṇā*: 1.28 Dhāraṇā is the binding of the mind to a particular location. The binding of the mind to a specific place within the body or elsewhere is called *dhāraṇā*. For example, the binding of the mind to the lotus of the heart, or to the navel, or to the crown of the head, or to the tip of the nose, or to the tip of the tongue, or to the space outside the body, and so forth. This is what is meant by *dhāraṇā*. 1.29 When there is steadiness of that [mind] in that [place], it is *dhyāna*. When the mind remains steady in that very place where it was bound, that state is called *dhyāna*. 1.30 When the object of meditation alone shines forth in that [state], devoid of the form of the knower and the act of knowing, that is *samādhi*. When, in that state of *dhyāna*, the object of meditation alone appears as if devoid of the forms of the subject and the process of cognition, that is *samādhi*. 1.31 These three together, applied to a single object, are called *saṃyama*. These three—*dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*—when directed toward a single object, are designated by the collective term *saṃyama*. 1.32 By mastery over this, the light of knowledge arises from within. From mastery over *saṃyama*, the light of knowledge arises from within the yogi himself. As the Lord says: "The light of knowledge born of *samādhi* shines forth. Just as a lamp placed in a windless spot does not flicker, so too the light of knowledge born of *samādhi* becomes steady. And by the steadiness of that light, the reality of things is perceived exactly as it is. Therefore, one should practice *saṃyama* on whatever object one desires to know. 1.33 Its application is before the *tāra* and the others. The application of this *saṃyama* is prior to the various supernormal powers such as *tāra*. That is to say, one should first practice *saṃyama* on the *tāra* and other such objects. Once proficiency in *saṃyama* has been achieved, one may then proceed to practice *saṃyama* on other objects. 1.34 It is not to be applied to the intermediate stages. This *saṃyama* is not to be applied to the intermediate stages (*antarāla*) between the *tāra* and the others. Why? Because those intermediate stages are not clearly defined. Since they are not clearly defined, one cannot practice *saṃyama* upon them. However, when the *tāra* and the others have become clearly manifest, one may then practice *saṃyama* upon them. 1.35 From that, the knowledge of another's mind. From *saṃyama* on the *tāra* and the others, the knowledge of another's mind arises. How? By practicing *saṃyama* on the *tāra*, one knows the *tāra* of another; by practicing *saṃyama* on the *vitarka*, one knows the *vitarka* of another; and so on. Thus, by practicing *saṃyama* on the *tāra* and the others, one gains knowledge of another's mind. 1.36 Not of its own mental impressions. One does not know the mental impressions of one's own mind through this [knowledge of another's mind]. Why? Because one's own mental impressions are not clearly manifest. Since they are not clearly manifest, one cannot know them. However, when one's own mental impressions become clearly manifest, then one knows them. 1.37 From *saṃyama* on the form, the disappearance of the veil of the light. From *saṃyama* on the form of the light, the veil covering that light disappears. What is this light? It is the power of consciousness. What is the veil? It is the karma accumulated through beginningless births. From *saṃyama* on the form of that light, the veil of karma is destroyed. When the veil is destroyed, the light shines forth. When the light shines forth, all things are perceived exactly as they are. Therefore, one should practice *saṃyama* on the form of the light. 1.38 From *saṃyama* on the sun, the knowledge of the worlds. From *saṃyama* on the sun, the knowledge of the worlds arises. Within the sun, there are seven worlds: Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, Satyaloka, Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and Svarloka. From *saṃyama* on the sun, the knowledge of these worlds arises. 1.39 From *saṃyama* on the moon, the knowledge of the stars. From *saṃyama* on the moon, the knowledge of the stars arises. Within the moon, there are thirty-three thousand and thirty-three hundred lunar mansions. From *saṃyama* on the moon, the knowledge of these arises. 1.40 From *saṃyama* on the pole star, the knowledge of their motions. From *saṃyama* on the pole star, the knowledge of the motions of the stars arises. Within the pole star, there is a fixed point of connection for the celestial bodies. From *saṃyama* on that point, the knowledge of their motions arises. 1.41 From *saṃyama* on the navel circle, the knowledge of the constitution of the body. From *saṃyama* on the navel circle, the knowledge of the constitution of the body arises. Within the navel circle, there is a wheel of twelve spokes. From *saṃyama* on that wheel, the knowledge of the constitution of the body arises. 1.42 From *saṃyama* on the throat-pit, the conquest of hunger and thirst. From *saṃyama* on the throat-pit, the conquest of hunger and thirst arises. Within the throat, there is a pit that obstructs the flow of food and drink. From *saṃyama* on that pit, hunger and thirst are conquered. 1.43 From *saṃyama* on the tortoise-nerve, steadiness. From *saṃyama* on the tortoise-nerve, steadiness arises. Within the body, there is a nerve shaped like a tortoise. From *saṃyama* on that nerve, the yogi attains steadiness. 1.44 From *saṃyama* on the light in the heart, the knowledge of the Self. From *saṃyama* on the light in the heart, the knowledge of the Self arises. Within the heart, there is a lotus. Within that lotus, there is a light. From *saṃyama* on that light, the knowledge of the Self arises. 1.45 Above the palate, the gate to the heavenly world. Above the palate, there is a gate leading to the heavenly world. From *saṃyama* on that gate, the yogi can enter the heavenly world. 1.46 From *saṃyama* on the channel of the throat, the disappearance of the covering of the voice. From *saṃyama* on the channel of the throat, the covering of the voice disappears. Within the throat, there is a channel that covers the voice. From *saṃyama* on that channel, the covering of the voice is removed, and the yogi's voice becomes divine. 1.47 From *saṃyama* on the radiance at the crown of the head, the vision of the Siddhas. From *saṃyama* on the radiance at the crown of the head, the vision of the Siddhas arises. At the crown of the head, there is a radiance. From *saṃyama* on that radiance, the yogi sees the Siddhas. 1.48 From *saṃyama* on the *prātibha*, the [supernatural] knowledge. From *saṃyama* on the *prātib
Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to a location; this is the first manifestation (*vibhūti*).

Regarding the function: the binding of the mind in a specific location, such as the navel-center, the tip of the nose, and so forth—its stabilization by means of abandoning other objects—is called concentration of the mind.

The meaning is this: by a yogi whose internal organ has been perfumed by the cultivation of a mind characterized by friendliness and so forth, who possesses the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), who has mastered posture (*āsana*), who has eliminated the distractions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and who has withdrawn the collection of the senses, steadiness of the mind must be achieved for the practice of cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) upon a spot such as the tip of the nose in an undisturbed place, with the body straight and the pairs of opposites conquered.
Having thus described *dhāraṇā*, he speaks in order to describe *dhyāna*: [Yoga Sūtra 3.2]...
In that context, meditation (*dhyāna*) is the one-pointedness of the cognitive flow (*pratyayaikatānatā*); this is the second manifestation of power.

"In that" means in that location where the mind has been fixed; "one-pointedness of the cognitive flow" refers to the continuous arising of knowledge (*jñāna*) by way of avoiding dissimilar transformations, such that whatever object was taken as the support during concentration (*dhāraṇā*), it arises uninterruptedly with that very same support—that is called meditation.
He describes the limb of yoga that is the final stage, meditative concentration (samādhi):
"That very [state] in which only the object appears, as if devoid of its own nature, is meditative concentration."

The third manifestation: That very meditation (*dhyāna*) characterized as previously described, wherein only the object appears—having emerged in the form of the object due to the absorption of the mental image of the object, and having its own nature as cognition become subordinate—attains, as it were, a state of being empty of its own nature; that is called *samādhi*.
It is so called because the mind is properly fixed (*sam-ā-dhīyate*) and made one-pointed there, having abandoned all distractions. Thus, it is *samādhi*.
In order to provide a technical (tāntrikī) designation for these three limbs of yoga whose characteristics have been stated, so that they may be used in his own treatise, he says:
"The three together constitute *saṃyama*."
Vibhūti 4: Vṛttiḥ — The triad of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi operating upon a single object is designated by the term "saṃyama" in the Śāstra.
He states its fruit: "From the conquest of that, there is the light of wisdom, which is sovereign power. (5)

Commentary: From the mastery of that *saṃyama*—through the cultivation of habituation and the production of naturalization—there arises the illumination, the outpouring, of wisdom (*prajñā*), which is discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*).
The meaning is that wisdom clearly illuminates the object of knowledge.
He states its application:
"Its application is in the stages;
[this is] the sixth [chapter on] manifestation."

Commentary: The application of that *saṃyama* must be made to the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) established upon the stages (*bhūmi*), according to the distinction between gross and subtle objects of support.
Having recognized each lower stage of the mind as conquered, one should practice *saṃyama* on the higher stage;
for he who has not mastered the lower stage becomes a partaker of the fruit only when practicing *saṃyama* on the higher stage.

In the sixth chapter, the *Sādhanapāda*, having enumerated the eight limbs of yoga and defined five of them, one might ask why [the definitions of] the remaining three were not provided. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The triad is internal compared to the preceding ones."

Commentary on Sūtra 7: Compared to the previously mentioned limbs of yoga, such as the restraints (yamas) and so forth, which assist samādhi only indirectly, the triad of limbs beginning with concentration (dhāraṇā)— namely concentration, meditation, and samādhi— is the "inner limb" of cognitive samādhi (samprajñāta-samādhi), because it brings about the actual realization of the nature of samādhi itself.
He states that even this is external in relation to another samādhi:
"That too is external to the seedless [samādhi], which is the sovereign power. (8)

Commentary: For the seedless samādhi—which is without objective support and is synonymous with the cultivation of emptiness—even these three limbs of yoga are external aids, because they are beneficial through a traditional succession.
Now, desiring to explain the perfections of yoga, he describes the threefold transformation in order to purify the object of *saṃyama*:

The transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*) consists in the suppression of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation, followed by the succession of moments of consciousness characterized by cessation; this is the ninth [topic], the function of supernormal power (*vibhūti*).—
Emergence (*vyutthāna*) refers to the three stages known as the distracted (*kṣipta*), the stupefied (*mūḍha*), and the occasionally distracted (*vikṣipta*).

Cessation is the transformation of the mind in which sattva predominates as its primary constituent. When there occurs, respectively, the suppression and the manifestation of the two impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those two— emergence and cessation—
suppression is their remaining in a state of subordination, being incapable of performing their function.

Manifestation (*prādurbhāva*) is the appearance [of a quality] in the present time by way of its form becoming evident. At that moment of cessation, because the mind exists across both moments, there is a continuity (*anvaya*); this is called the transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*).

The meaning is as follows: when the property (*dharma*) consisting of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the emergent state becomes concealed and the property consisting of the latent impression of cessation becomes manifest, and although the mind—by virtue of being the substratum (*dharmin*)—continues to persist through both, it is perceived as abiding in the nature of cessation; at that time, it is designated by the term "transformation of cessation."
Although there is no immobility of the mind because the functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile, nevertheless, a transformation of this kind is called steadiness (*sthairya*).
He states the fruit of that very [steadiness]:
The manifestation of its power is the state of tranquil flow resulting from mental impressions;
that is, through the aforementioned impressions of cessation, the mind attains a state of tranquil flow.
The meaning is that, by being free from distraction, the mind becomes transformed into a continuous flow of similar states.
Having described the transformation of cessation, he now speaks of the transformation of meditative concentration (samādhi):

The transformation of the mind through concentration (*samādhi*) consists in the cessation of its state of being directed toward all objects and the arising of one-pointedness; this is the manifestation of power.
Regarding the function: "being directed toward all objects" is a property of the mind characterized by distraction, due to its mobility, whereby it grasps various kinds of objects.
One-pointedness is the state of being transformed into similarity upon a single object;
this too is a property (*dharma*) of the mind.

The destruction and arising of these two, respectively—the destruction of the property characterized by "all-object-ness" (*sarvārthatā*) which is its utter suppression, and the manifestation or appearance of the property characterized by one-pointedness—is called the transformation of concentration (*samādhi-pariṇāma*), occurring as the persistence of the intensified essence (*sattva*) of the mind through its continuity.

The distinction between this [state] and the previous transformation is as follows: in that case, there was the suppression and manifestation of two factors characterized by *saṃskāra*—the subsiding of the former, which consists of the *saṃskāra* of emergence (*vyutthāna*), and the arising and non-suppressed persistence of the latter, which consists of the *saṃskāra* of cessation (*nirodha*).

Here, however, there is "destruction" (*kṣaya*) and "arising" (*udaya*): the destruction of distraction, whose nature is to pervade all states, is its absolute suppression and non-recurrence, its entry into the past time-track; the arising of the factor characterized by one-pointedness is its manifestation in the present time-track.
He states the third transformation of one-pointedness:
"The transformation of one-pointedness of the mind consists of the tranquil and the arisen being identical cognitions" (Yoga Sūtra 3.12).
This is the [twelfth] supernormal power (*vibhūti*).

Commentary: For the mind that is indeed in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*), there is a specific modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of a single cognition. One [cognition] has entered the past time-path and is stilled; the other has arisen and is manifest in the present time-path.
Both, by virtue of the mind being in a state of absorption, are equal and similar cognitions because they have an identical object of focus.
In both cases, the persistence of the concentrated mind itself as a continuous flow is called the transformation into one-pointedness (ekāgratā-pariṇāma).
Extending the description of the transformation of form (rūpa) stated for the mind to other cases as well, he says:
"By this, the transformations of property (dharma), characteristic (lakṣaṇa), and state (avasthā) regarding the elements (bhūta) and the sense organs (indriya) are explained" (Vibhūti 13).

Commentary: By this threefold transformation of the mind that has been described, one should understand that a threefold transformation is explained as occurring in the elements—both gross and subtle—and in the sense organs, which exist through the distinction of the intellect (*buddhi*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This occurs by way of the distinctions of quality (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*). The transformation of quality (*dharmapariṇāma*) is the emergence of a different quality upon the cessation of a previous quality of a persisting substrate (*dharmī*). For example, when a substrate characterized as clay abandons its quality of being a lump and assumes another quality of being a jar, this is called the transformation of quality.
Transformation of refinement (*lakṣṇapariṇāma*) is as follows: that very jar, by relinquishing its future temporal state (*adhvan*), assumes its present temporal state;
and by relinquishing that, it takes on its past temporal state.

Transformation of state (*avasthāpariṇāma*) is as follows: that very jar, through its persistence (*anvayitva*) across two similar moments characterized by time, such as the first and second [moments].

And since the functioning of qualities does not exist even for a moment without undergoing transformation, one might ask: "What, then, is this substratum (dharmin)? Anticipating this doubt, he states the definition of the substratum:
The substrate (dharmin) conforms to attributes (dharmas) that are quiescent, emergent, or unmanifest; this is its manifestation.
Regarding the function: those attributes which have performed their respective operations and entered the past time-path are quiescent.

Those [entities] that have arisen and, having abandoned the future time, perform their own functions in the present time; those which are "indesignatable" (avyapadeśya), meaning they exist in the form of potentiality (śakti) and cannot be designated—they possess, each according to its own nature, the state of being composed of all things. It is precisely this potentiality (śakti), as delimited by the fitness for specific cause-and-effect relationships, that is denoted here by the word *dharma*.

That which follows, conforms to, and accepts all three kinds of attributes (dharma) by way of persistence is called the "substratum possessing attributes" (dharmī) that conforms to past, present, and future attributes.

For example, when gold abandons the attribute of being a bracelet and assumes another attribute in the form of a svastika, it persists as gold; while those attributes are in some sense distinct, it appears as a persisting entity through its nature as the substratum, existing as a universal in the form of the substratum and as particulars in the form of the attributes.
To dispel the doubt as to how there can be multiple transformations of a single substrate (dharmin), he says:
"The difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation" (Vibhūti 15).

Commentary: Regarding the sequence of phenomena whose characteristics have been stated, the observed difference at every moment serves as the cause, the mark, and the indicator of the transformation (*pariṇāma*) whose characteristics have been stated—that is, its manifoldness and difference.

The meaning is this: this fixed sequence that is observed—such as from clay powder comes a lump of clay, from that shards, and from those a jar—is of the nature of a sequence and makes known the difference within transformation.

In that very same substratum (dharmin), the sequence of the transformation of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma) and the transformation of states (avasthā-pariṇāma) is also to be understood as an indicator of the distinctness of these transformations by this very same principle. For all entities are observed to transform at every moment according to a fixed sequence;
therefore, it is established that because the sequences are distinct, the transformations are distinct.
Among all the transforming phenomena such as the mind and so forth, some dharmas are perceived directly,
such as pleasure and the like, as well as shape and the like;
others are exclusively to be known through inference.
Just as the capacity for the formation of dharmas and so forth, along with the substratum itself, follow through everything by way of being both distinct and non-distinct in nature. 15
Now, in order to demonstrate the perfections (*siddhi*) by way of showing the objects of the aforementioned restraint (*saṃyama*), he says:
"From *saṃyama* on the threefold transformation, there is knowledge of the past and the future" (Sūtra 16).

Commentary: Regarding the threefold transformation that has been described through the distinctions of dharma, characteristic, and state—by means of *saṃyama* (mastery) upon that object, that is, by performing the aforementioned *saṃyama* with respect to it, knowledge of the past and future arises for the yogin from *samādhi*.

This is the essential meaning here: when one practices *saṃyama* with a mind free from distraction—thinking that "this attribute, this characteristic, and this state of this subject, having come from the future path, perform its own function in the present path, and then enter the past path"—then the yogi knows everything, whether it be yet unarisen or already passed away.
This is because the capacity of the mind to grasp all objects, which consists of the radiance of pure *sattva*, is impaired by distractions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like.

But when distractions are avoided by those various means, then, like a mirror from which impurities have been removed, the capacity to apprehend all objects manifests through the power of one-pointedness.
He states another accomplishment:
Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is a confusion among them; by practicing *saṃyama* on their distinction, there arises the knowledge of the cries of all beings.

(Sūtra 17) Commentary: A "word" (*śabda*) is that which is perceivable by the sense of hearing, consisting of phonemes arranged in a fixed sequence, and delimited by the comprehension of a specific meaning.
Whether it be the nature of *sphoṭa* devoid of sequential order, which is apprehended by an intellect refined by the scriptures,

or both [the sequential and non-sequential forms]— in either case, it exists in the form of words (*pada*) and sentences (*vākya*). Since they possess the capacity for the comprehension of a single meaning,
the "meaning" (*artha*) consists of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and so forth.
The *pratyaya* (cognition) is the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) taking on the form of the object; it is knowledge.

In common usage, these—word, object, and cognition—are conflated because, despite being distinct, they are brought to a state of apparent unity through mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*). To illustrate: when one says, "Bring the cow," someone perceives the object characterized as a cow—that is, a physical mass possessing a dewlap and defined by the universal of cowness—as non-different from the word that denotes it and the cognition that grasps it. He does not, however, conduct his affairs by distinguishing them as: "the word 'cow' is the denoter, this [object] is the denoted, and this is the cognition that grasps those two."
For instance, when asked, "What is this object?", "What is this word?", or "What is this cognition?", he gives an answer of a single uniform nature in every case, namely, "A cow.
If he did not apprehend a single uniform nature, how could he provide an answer of a single uniform nature?

When that [sound] has been established in this way, there is this distinction: this is the essence of sound, namely its capacity as a signifier (*vācakatva*); this is the essence of the object, namely its capacity as the signified (*vācyatva*); and this is the essence of cognition, namely its capacity as an illuminator (*prakāśakatva*). Having made this distinction, he who applies *saṃyama* to that distinction gains knowledge of the cries of all beings—beasts, birds, reptiles, and so forth.
With this very intention, he knows everything: "This sound was uttered by this particular living being. (17)
He states another perfection: "From the direct perception of latent impressions (saṃskāra), there is knowledge of previous births" (Yoga Sūtra 3.18).
Commentary: There are two kinds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the form of tendencies (*vāsanā*) within the mind:

some have as their result the mere production of memory, while others are causes of fruition (*vipāka*), characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience—such as those called merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*).

When one practices *saṃyama* upon these latent impressions, recollecting and contemplating previous occurrences in this way—"Thus was that object experienced by me" or "Thus was that action accomplished by me"—one whose latent impressions have been awakened even without an external stimulus remembers everything past.
When the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been awakened and realized in succession, one perceives even the birth and other factors experienced in previous lives through direct perception.
He states another accomplishment (*siddhi*):
The supernormal power (vibhūti) regarding the cognition of another's mind is the function [of saṃyama] 19.

When one practices saṃyama upon the cognition of another's mind— which has been grasped through some sign such as the color of the face— then knowledge of that other's mind arises, [discerning] whether "this person's mind is possessed of passion" or "free from passion."
The meaning is that he knows all phenomena (dharmas) contained within the minds of others.
He now states the specific knowledge regarding this very knowledge of others' minds:

And that [other mind] cannot be known as having an object (*sālambana*), because it has not become an object for that [knowing mind]. This is the function of mastery (verse 20): that mind of another person, which possesses an object, cannot be known together with its own object, because the object has not been made an object by any sign (*liṅga*).
For from the indicative mark (liṅga), only the mere mind of another is understood, but not that "this person's mind has blue as its object" or "it has yellow as its object.

Since it is impossible to perform *saṃyama* upon that which has not been grasped, there can be no knowledge of the specific object of another's mind. Therefore, another's mind is not perceived together with its objective support (*ālambana*), because that objective support remains ungrasped.
Furthermore, mental states (cittadharmas) are indeed perceived;
however, when one forms the resolve, "What has this [mind] taken as its object?", then through mastery over that [resolve], knowledge regarding that object also certainly arises.
He states another perfection:
"From *saṃyama* on the form of the body, when the power of its being perceived is suppressed and there is no conjunction with the light of the eye, [there is] invisibility" (Sūtra 21).

Commentary: "Body" (kāya) means the physical frame; its "form" (rūpa) is the quality perceivable by the eye. Through *saṃyama* upon that form—meaning, "there is form in this body"—when there is a suppression, that is, a blocking by the power of cultivation, of that power which consists in the form's being perceivable by the eye, and when there is no conjunction of the light of the eye with that [form], then because the eye's light—which is a property of *sattva*—is not in conjunction, and thus lacks the activity of perceiving it, the yogi achieves invisibility;
the meaning is that he is not seen by anyone.

By this very demonstration of the means for the disappearance of form, it should be understood that the disappearance of sound and the other objects perceivable by the ear and the other senses has also been explained.
He now states another accomplishment:

Karma is both with-impetus (sopakrama) and without-impetus (nirupakrama); through mastery over it, or by means of portents (ariṣṭas), there arises knowledge of the final end [of life]. Commentary: That karma performed previously which ripens as lifespan is of two kinds: with-impetus and without-impetus.

In that regard, "action with effort" (*sopakrama*) is that which proceeds toward the performance of its effect together with an impulse for the production of its fruit; for example, a wet cloth spread out in a warm place dries very quickly. The opposite of what has been stated is "action without effort" (*nirupakrama*); for example, that same wet cloth, when folded up in a non-warm place, dries after a long time.

Regarding these two kinds of action, he who practices *saṃyama*—asking, "Is my action one of quick fruition or of slow fruition?"—attains knowledge of the future through the firmness of his meditation.

The future limit is the separation from the body; he knows with certainty, "At such a time and in such a place, my separation from the body will occur," either through signs of death (*ariṣṭa*)— which are of three kinds— or otherwise.
There are internal, external, and celestial [obstacles].

Among these, the internal are such as when one whose sense organs are obstructed does not hear the sound of the wind within the abdomen, and so forth. The external are such as the sudden sight of a deformed person, and so forth.

Supernatural portents (*ādhidaivika*)—such as the sudden appearance of objects like heaven that are otherwise impossible to see—allow one to know the time of separation from the body. Although such knowledge generally arises for non-yogins through these omens (*ariṣṭas*), it occurs for them only in a general form and is of a doubtful nature; however, for yogins, it is certain regarding place and time, and is unerring, like direct perception.
In order to demonstrate the accomplishments (siddhi) brought about by the preparatory practices (parikarman), he says:
"The powers (bala) in [the four immeasurables] such as loving-kindness."
Vibhūti 23: Commentary—Through the practice of *saṃyama* upon friendliness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), powers related to these qualities arise.
Thus, his friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity reach such a height that he perceives the state of being a friend and so forth toward all beings.
He states another accomplishment:
"Among the powers, [there are] those such as the power of the hand," and so forth.
Commentary on Vibhūti 24: For one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the powers associated with elephants and so forth, those powers—namely the powers of elephants and the like—become manifest.

The meaning of this is as follows: when he practices *saṃyama* through identification (*tanmayībhāva*) with a particular elephant-force, or the speed of the wind, or the prowess of a lion, a *sattva* (mental essence) endowed with that specific capacity manifests for him. This is the sense.
He states another accomplishment:
"From the application of the light of the outgoing breath, there is knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the distant."
Vibhūti 25: Commentary— The outward-turned activity (*pravṛtti*) directed toward objects and that which is luminous (*jyotiṣmatī*) were previously described [in Sūtras 1.35–36].

Through the placement of its light—the sattvic illumination—upon all objects, and through the contemplation of those objects thus permeated, knowledge arises within the internal organ and the senses—which have attained superior power—regarding the extremely subtle, such as atoms; regarding the obstructed, such as treasures buried underground; and regarding the remote, such as elixirs located on the far side of Mount Meru.
To establish another instance of a similar occurrence, he says:
Through *saṃyama* on the sun, knowledge of the worlds [arises]; this is the twenty-sixth supernormal power (*vibhūti*).

Commentary: For one who performs *saṃyama* on the sun, which consists of light, there arises in him, exactly as it is, knowledge of the worlds (*bhuvana*)—the cities possessing their respective configurations—located within the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.
In the previous sūtra, sattvic light was described as the object;
here, however, the distinction is that it is elemental (bhautika).
He states another accomplishment by means of taking various physical lights as objects:
"Knowledge of the array of stars in the moon is a supernatural power" (27).
Commentary: Through *saṃyama* performed upon the moon, knowledge arises regarding the specific arrangement—that is, the particular configuration—of the stars, which are luminous bodies.
Since the stars have their brilliance eclipsed by the light of the sun, such knowledge of them cannot be attained through *saṃyama* on the sun; therefore, this separate means has been taught. (27)
He states another accomplishment:
"Knowledge of its motion in the fixed [pole star] is a supernatural power" (28).

Commentary: For one who has performed *saṃyama* upon the polar star (*dhruva*), the immovable preeminent light among the luminaries, there arises knowledge of the movement of those stars—each having a specific time and a specific location. He knows everything: "This is that star; this is that planet; after such a length of time, it will reach this zodiac sign or this lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
This is said to be the fruit of the knowledge of time. (28)
Having established the external accomplishments, he begins to establish the internal accomplishments:
"Knowledge of the array of bodies in the navel-cakra is the twenty-ninth manifestation."

Commentary: For the yogi who has performed *saṃyama* upon that sixteen-spoked wheel known as the *nābhi* (navel) situated within the body, there arises knowledge regarding the "arrangement" (*vyūha*)—the specific disposition—of the channels (*nāḍī*), humors (*dhātu*), and other constituents located within the body.
This is what is meant: the navel-wheel, situated in the center of the body, is the root-source of the channels and so forth that radiate in all directions;
therefore, for one who has fixed their attention there, the entire configuration appears exactly as it is.
He states another accomplishment:
the cessation of hunger and thirst in the pit of the throat (kaṇṭhakūpa).

Commentary on Sūtra 30: The "throat-pit" (kaṇṭhakūpa) is a pit at the base of the throat, beneath the root of the tongue, shaped like a hollow. When a yogi performs *saṃyama* upon that spot—whereby hunger, thirst, and other such states arise through contact with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth—hunger, thirst, and the rest cease for him.
When that [wind] is held by the stream below the uvula (ghaṇṭikā) and cultivated, such an accomplishment (siddhi) indeed occurs.
He states another accomplishment:
Stability through the tortoise-channel (kūrmanāḍī) is the thirty-first manifestation:
stability arises for the mind when restraint is applied to the channel called "tortoise" (kūrma), which is located below the pit of the throat (kaṇṭhakūpa).
The meaning is that for one who has entered that state, there is no longer any restlessness; or rather, the meaning is that steadiness of the body arises such that it cannot be moved by anything.
He states another accomplishment:
"The vision of perfected beings in the light at the crown of the head is a supernatural power" (32).

Commentary: In the aperture of the skull known as the *brahmarandhra*, which is a light because it is the locus of illumination—just as the radiance of a gem situated inside a house spreads out and appears as if gathered into a curved form in every direction—so too the sattvic light residing in the heart, having spread forth, attains a state of condensation there.

For one who has performed *saṃyama* upon that [aperture], there arises the vision of those divine beings, the perfected ones (*siddhas*) dwelling in the space between heaven and earth, who are invisible to other living beings.
The meaning is that he sees them and converses with them.
He now states the means for attaining omniscience:
Or, everything arises from intuition (*prātibha*).
[Commentary on Sūtra 33: Intuition (*pratibhā*) is knowledge that arises suddenly, is non-contradictory, and is produced by the mind alone, independent of external causes.

When that *saṃyama* is practiced, the "saving" (*tāraka*) knowledge arises, which precedes discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). Just as light appears before the sun is about to rise, so too does this saving knowledge—which has all things as its object—arise prior to discriminative discernment.
When that knowledge exists, one knows everything without depending on other forms of *saṃyama*; such is the meaning.
33. He states another accomplishment: "In the heart, the consciousness of the mind."
Commentary on Verse 34: The heart is a specific region of the body;
within it, inside a small lotus facing downward, is the location of the *sattva* of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
In that state, for one who has practiced self-restraint, the knowledge of one's own and others' minds arises;
the meaning is that one knows all latent impressions (vāsanās) residing in one's own mind as well as passion and other states residing in the minds of others.

He states another perfection: "Experience is the non-differentiation of the cognitions of the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely distinct; from saṃyama on that which is other than the object-for-others as being for one's own sake, there arises knowledge of the puruṣa" (Sūtra 3.35).
Commentary: *Sattva* is a specific transformation of *pradhāna*, consisting of luminosity and pleasure;
the *puruṣa* is the enjoyer, whose nature is that of a presiding witness.

Since these two are absolutely unmixed—being distinct by virtue of being the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer, and by virtue of being insentient and sentient—the non-distinction of their cognition, which is the failure to perceive them as separate, results in the experience of pleasure and pain through the attribution of agency to *sattva* alone; that is *bhoga* (enjoyment).

The purpose of another (the Spirit) for the sake of the *sattva* is independent of its own self-interest; distinct from that is the self-interest [of the *sattva*] which has as its sole object the true nature of the Spirit (*puruṣasvarūpamātra*). When the *sattva* has abandoned egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), there occurs a transfer of the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) into it. For one who practices *saṃyama* upon this, knowledge having the Spirit as its object arises. The meaning is that the Spirit knows that very knowledge—which has itself as its object and is established in the *sattva*.

Furthermore, the person who is the knower does not become an object of knowledge, because that would entail being an object of cognition, and there is an absolute contradiction between the state of being a knower and the state of being an object of knowledge.
He states the fruit of this very *saṃyama*: [35]
From that, intuitive perception, hearing, touch, sight, taste, and awareness arise as manifestations (vibhūti).
[Sūtra 36] — From that, through the practice of *saṃyama* upon the *puruṣa*, various forms of knowledge arise even for one who has emerged from meditative absorption.
In this context, "intuitive" (prātibha) refers to the previously mentioned knowledge; through its manifestation, one perceives subtle and other such objects.
"Auditory" (śrāvaṇa) is the knowledge born of the sense of hearing, and through that, one knows divine sound which is superior [to ordinary sound].
"Sensory" (vedanā) is the knowledge born of the sense of touch; it is designated by this technical (tāntrikī) term because it is "that by which something is felt" (vedyate anayā).
Therefore, knowledge having divine touch as its object arises.
A mirror is knowledge born of the eye-faculty;
because form is seen and experienced by it all around, through its excellence, divine knowledge of form arises.
Taste is the cognition produced by the gustatory faculty,
so called because it is "tasted" by means of this; when that [faculty] is preeminent, a consciousness of divine flavor arises,
and from that comes the consciousness of fragrance.
By the word *vṛtti*, according to the technical terminology of the Tantras, the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya*) is meant;
since it functions (*vartate*) with respect to the object of smell, the news (*vārtā*) arising from that olfactory organ—namely, the perception of smell—is called *vārtā*.
When that perception is intensified, divine fragrance is experienced.
He states the division of the spheres for these specific fruits:
"These are obstacles in meditative concentration (samādhi), but they are accomplishments (siddhis) in the state of emergence (vyutthāna)."
Commentary on Vibhūti 37: Those specific fruits previously explained become obstacles, calamities, and hindrances as one advances toward the excellence of samādhi;
therein, by giving rise to joy, pride, and so forth, the samādhi becomes slackened.
However, upon emerging— during the state of ordinary worldly activity— they become *siddhis* because they bestow specific fruits.
He states another *siddhi*:

Entry into another's body occurs through the loosening of the causes of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind; this is the thirty-eighth supernormal power (*vibhūti*).—Because the self and the mind are all-pervading, their state as enjoyer and enjoyed arises only within a body due to the force of specific karma; that very [state] is called "bondage to the body."
Thus, when the cause of bondage known as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) becomes loosened and reaches attenuation through the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*),

and when there occurs the perception— that is, the knowledge— of that movement of the mind which flows out toward objects through the doors of the senses by entering the heart; this is the channel (*nāḍī*) called *cittavahā*,
by which the mind flows.

And this [power] is distinct from the channels that carry the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—when one knows how to move between one's own body and another's, one enters a dead or living body belonging to another by means of the movement of the mind;

and as the mind enters the other's body, the sense organs follow it, just as bees follow the king bee. Then, having entered the other's body, the yogi conducts all his affairs through it as if through his own body.

Since karma is the cause for the restriction of experience (bhoga) for the two pervasive entities— the mind and the person— if that karma is cast off by means of meditative absorption (samādhi), then, through its own sovereignty, the accomplishment of experience occurs everywhere.
He states another supernatural power (siddhi):

Through mastery over *udāna*, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of *utkrānti* (ejection from the body); this is the thirty-ninth supernormal power (*vibhūti*).
As for the commentary: the simultaneous activity of all the sense organs, which arises like the simultaneous flash of sparks from [beaten] grain-husks, is designated by the term "life" (*jīvana*).
Due to the differentiation of its functions, it is designated by various names such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth.
Among these, because the wind moves upward from the heart through the openings of the mouth and nose, it is called *prāṇa*;
because it leads [the breath] downward from the region of the navel to the tips of the big toes, it is called *apāna*.
The *samāna* [vital air] is so called because it winds around the region of the navel on all sides;
the *udāna* is so called because it rises upward from the nape of the neck to the top of the head;
and the *vyāna* is so called because it pervades the entire body by spreading throughout it.

Therein, by means of mastery over *udāna* through the door of *saṃyama*, because the other vital airs (*vāyu*) are obstructed, one moves upward; thus, one does not sink in water such as a great river or in thick mud, nor among sharp thorns, due to extreme lightness like a tuft of cotton.
The meaning is that even when immersed in water and so forth, one rises up.
He states another accomplishment:
"From mastery over the *samāna* [vital air], there is blazing; this is a supernatural power (vibhūti). 40

Commentary: By means of *saṃyama*—that is, through mastery—over the wind called *samāna*, which is situated surrounding the fire, the fire becomes unobstructed; consequently, the yogi appears as if blazing with radiance.
He states another perfection: 40.

Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing arises—this is the [forty-first] supernormal power (*vibhūti*). Commentary: The ear is the organ belonging to the *ahaṃkāra*, which perceives sound.
Space (*ākāśa*) is the ether (*vyoman*), which is the effect of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*).

The relationship between these two is characterized by that of location and the occupant of the location. For the yogi who has practiced *saṃyama* upon this [relationship], divine hearing (*divya-śrotra*) comes forth;
the meaning is that it becomes capable of simultaneously perceiving sounds that are subtle, obstructed, or distant.
He states another perfection:
"From *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and from mastery (*samāpatti*) over lightness like that of cotton, there is the power of moving through space."
Vibhūti 42: Commentary—The body is the physical frame composed of the five elements.

Having performed *saṃyama* upon the connection that this body has with space, which provides it with room, and having achieved *samāpatti*—characterized by becoming one with the object—in something light such as cotton, the yogi who has attained extreme lightness first moves through water according to his desire, then proceeds by means of a web of spider-silk threads, and finally travels through space at will, moving among the rays of the sun.
He states another perfection:
"The external, non-imagined state is the 'Great Bodiless' (mahāvidehā); from that follows the destruction of the veil over light."

Vibhūti 43: Vṛtti—That activity of the mind which occurs outside the body, independent of the body, is called Mahāvideha; it is said to be that state in which the momentum of the effects of egoism has departed. Through saṃyama performed upon that [state], there is the destruction of the covering of light. That is to say, the destruction—the dissolution—of the covering of the sattvic mind’s light, which consists of afflictions, karma, and so forth.
This is the meaning: when there is the ego-identification with the body, whatever outward activity of the mind occurs is called "imagined" (kalpita).
However, when the mind's activity occurs independently, having abandoned the state of ego-identification with the body, that is "unimagined" (akalpita).
