Through *saṃyama* upon this [unimagined state], all impurities of the yogi’s mind are destroyed.

43. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound prajñāpāramitā, illuminates and delivers those who practice on the bodhisattva path. At that time, the Bhagavat was in Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the Bhagavat addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "If the venerable Śāriputra wishes to see the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, he should contemplate the profound prajñāpāramitā. Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Buddha: "O Bhagavat, how should a son of good family who wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā train? The Buddha told Śāriputra: "A son of good family who wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā should observe that all phenomena are empty in their own nature. Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are empty, without characteristics, unproduced, undestroyed, stainless, and not stainless, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomenon; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a bodhisattva relies on prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams, one attains ultimate nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, by relying on prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true, not false. Thus the mantra of prajñāpāramitā is spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Buddha: "O Bhagavat, how wonderful! How rare! This profound prajñāpāramitā is the teacher of the teachers of the three worlds. All the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot understand it. Why? O Bhagavat, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family accepts, holds, reads, recites, and explains this profound prajñāpāramitā to others, the Bhagavat should know that such a person has already made offerings to many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas. O Bhagavat, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family accepts, holds, reads, recites, and explains this profound prajñāpāramitā to others, they will not be harmed by yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, or humans and non-humans. Why? Because the profound prajñāpāramitā is the great protection, the great refuge, and the great consolation for all sentient beings. Thus, having established the accomplishments (*siddhi*) pertaining to the past limit, the future limit, and the intermediate state, [the author] now explains those accomplishments—such as the knowledge of the worlds and so forth—which are external; those such as the multiplication of bodies (*kāyavyūha*) and so forth, which are internal; and those consisting of the powers (*bala*) of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest, which are perfected through preparatory rites (*parikarman*). Furthermore, he explains those arising from the senses characterized by the internal and external organs, and those arising from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, for the sake of strengthening the mind and generating confidence in *samādhi*. Now, in order to demonstrate various means for the attainment of the seeded (*sabīja*) and seedless (*nirbīja*) *samādhi* useful for his own philosophical system, he says:
Mastery over the elements results from *saṃyama* upon their gross form, subtle essence, inherence, and purposefulness.

(Sūtra 44) Commentary: Regarding the five elements, earth and the rest, there are five properties consisting of specific states, such as grossness and so forth. For one who has performed *saṃyama* upon these, mastery over the elements (*bhūtajaya*) occurs.
The meaning is that the elements (bhūtas) become subject to his control;
for instance, the gross form of the elements, which is perceived as possessing specific shapes,
consists of five essential natures whose effects are, respectively, fragrance, moisture, heat, motion, and the provision of space.

Furthermore, the subtle elements—the *tanmātras* of smell and so forth—are established as the causes of the gross elements in their respective order; these are the pervasive qualities (*guṇas*) which are perceived everywhere as being present through their nature of illumination, activity, and stability.
Their "possessiveness of purpose" (*arthavattva*) consists in the power inherent in those very qualities to accomplish experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).

Thus, when the five elements are distinguished by the aforementioned characteristics, states, and conditions, the yogi who applies *saṃyama* to each state individually becomes a master of the elements (*bhūtajayin*).

This is as follows: first, having performed *saṃyama* on the gross form, and subsequently on the essential nature (*svarūpa*), in this sequence, the primal natures of the elements come to follow his will, just as cows follow their calves; such is the meaning. 44
He states the fruit of that very mastery over the elements:
"From that, there is the manifestation of [powers] such as atomization (aṇimā), perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by its properties; this is sovereign power. (4.5)
Commentary: 1. *Aṇimā* is the attainment of the state of being atomic in form. 2. [The second power is *laghimā*, the attainment of extreme lightness.]
Mahimā is the attainment of greatness;
laghimā is the attainment of lightness like a tuft of cotton.
Garimā is the attainment of heaviness.
Attainment (prāpti) is the power of touching the moon and other distant objects with the tip of a finger;
irresistible will (prākāmya) is the non-obstruction of one's desire.
Sovereignty (īśitva) is the state of being the lord of the body and the internal organ.
Omnipotence is mastery;
because it follows after all beings, they do not transgress what has been spoken.

"Where there is the fulfillment of desire" means that in whatever object the yogi has a desire—that is, a wish according to his own will—therein occurs his firm resolve (*adhyavasāya*); the meaning is that he leads that object to the completion of his longing by way of its acquisition.
These [powers], beginning with *aṇimā*, which are useful for meditative absorption (*samādhi*), manifest for the yogi through the mastery of the elements (*bhūtajaya*).
Just as one who has attained the state of an atom enters even into diamonds and the like, so it should be applied in all cases;
these eight qualities, beginning with *aṇimā*, are called the great accomplishments (*mahāsiddhi*).
The perfection of the body (*kāyasampad*) will be explained [later]; he attains that, as well as the non-affliction of its qualities.

Regarding "the non-affliction of its qualities": for those qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth belonging to that body, there is no affliction—that is, no destruction—from anything whatsoever. It should be applied thus: "fire does not burn his form, nor does wind dry it up," and so forth.
He speaks of the perfection of the body: the perfection of the body consists of beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine firmness.
Vibhūti 46: Commentary—Beauty, grace, and strength are well known;
"vajra-like compactness" means that his body possesses a firm and solid structure like a diamond.
Thus ends the perfection of manifested qualities of the body (46).
Having thus described the conquest of the elements (*bhūtajaya*), he now speaks of the conquest of the senses (*indriyajaya*) for one who has attained the specific stages (*bhūmikā*):
Through *saṃyama* on perception, its essential nature, egoism, succession, and purposefulness, mastery over the senses is attained.
(Sūtra 4.7) Commentary: Perception (*grahaṇa*) is the function of the senses directed toward their respective objects.
Its essential nature is luminosity in a general sense;
its self-sense (*asmitā*) is the persistence of the notion of "I"; and its pervasive existence and purposefulness are as explained previously. (3)
44) By performing *saṃyama* as previously described upon these five states of the senses, one becomes a conqueror of the senses.
He states its fruit:
"From that come the power of moving with the speed of mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over primordial matter; these are the sovereign powers.
The commentary: Manojavitva is the attainment of unsurpassed speed for the body, like that of the mind; Vikaraṇabhāva is the attainment of the functioning of the senses independently of the body;
and Sarvavaśitva is mastery over Pradhāna.
These perfections manifest for one who has conquered the senses,

and they are called "Honey-like" (*madhupratīkā*) in this treatise; just as even a single portion of honey is sweet, so too each of these perfections is individually sweet— thus they are "Honey-like."
Having described the conquest of the senses, he speaks of the conquest of the internal organs:
for one who possesses the mere discriminative discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there arises sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience.

Vibhūti-pāda, Sūtra 49—Commentary: When one practices *saṃyama* upon that sattvic transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*), there arises a discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa, consisting in the loosening of the identification with agency attributed to the *guṇas*. By virtue of that [discernment], for the yogi established in that very state, there arise from *samādhi* both universal sovereignty and omniscience.
Universal sovereignty over all modifications of the *guṇas* and all existing things means having mastery over them as if one were their master.
And for those very [guṇas] which exist as the substrates characterized by being quiescent, emergent, or unmanifest, the discriminative knowledge of them exactly as they are constitutes omniscience;
and when the supreme state known as "mastery" has been attained in this treatise, it is called the perfection named "freedom from sorrow.
He states the next stage in sequence:
"From detachment even from that, upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (kaivalya). (Sūtra 50)

Commentary: Even regarding that sorrowless perfection (*viśokā siddhi*), when detachment arises in the yogi, then, upon the destruction—that is, the uprooting—of the seed of those defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which is ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest, there occurs *kaivalya*, the absolute cessation of suffering for the person (*puruṣa*). This is the state of being established in one's own nature (*svarūpapratiṣṭhatva*) once the duty (*adhikāra*) of the *guṇas* has been fully accomplished.
(50) Regarding that very same meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he states the means for its stability:
When invited by a sovereign, one should avoid attachment and pride, lest there be the recurrence of undesirable consequences. [This is] the commentary on verse 51: there are four types of yogis.
Among them, the first is the one possessed of practice whose light has merely begun to function;
the second is the one whose wisdom bears truth (*ṛtambhara-prajña*);
the third is the one who has conquered the elements and the senses.
The fourth [stage] is that which has transcended what is to be cultivated;

therein, one who has attained the wisdom reaching the limit of the sevenfold stages of the fourth samādhi becomes a master who realizes the second stage, known as "Honeyed" (*madhumatī*), for whom the gods become offerers of invitations.
They offer celestial women, elixirs, and other such things; toward such an invitation, he should neither form an attachment nor feel pride.

For by forming an attachment, he falls again into the enjoyment of sense objects, and by feeling pride—thinking himself to have accomplished all that was to be done—he no longer exerts himself in *samādhi*.
Therefore, he must avoid both attachment and pride.
Regarding this very discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which is the fruit [of yoga], he states another means distinct from the previously mentioned *saṃyama*:
"From *saṃyama* on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discrimination arises."

Vibhūti 52: The commentary states— through *saṃyama* upon the sequence, that is, the successive transformation in the order of priority and posteriority, of those moments of time which are the ultimate constituents of time and whose further subdivisions cannot be discerned, there arises the previously mentioned knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*).

The meaning is this: when one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon such a sequence—as "this momentary characteristic (*kālakṣaṇa*) is subsequent to that momentary characteristic" and "this is prior to that"—attains direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) even of the extremely subtle sequence of moments, then he also perceives other subtle things, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth; thus, discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) arises.
(52) To introduce the discernment of objects for this very *saṃyama*, he says:
Because difference is not delimited by genus, characteristic, or location, there is consequently the cognition of two things as equal; this is the function of manifestation (vibhūti).
The causes of distinction among objects are genus, characteristic, and location.
In some cases, the cause of distinction is the genus (*jāti*),
as in "this is a cow" and "this is a buffalo," where the genus is the cause of distinction between two things that are otherwise similar in their characteristics.
It is observed that place is the cause of distinction between two things that are indistinguishable by species or characteristic— such as this one being variegated and that one being red—
just as in the case of two myrobalan fruits of equal size situated in different places.

Furthermore, when a distinction cannot otherwise be determined—as in the case of two white, earthy atoms situated in the same place—knowledge of the distinction arises for one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon such an object; through that practice, one perceives even subtle principles as distinct.
This is what is meant: where a distinction cannot be determined by any other means, the realization of that distinction occurs precisely through *saṃyama*.
In order to explain that the knowledge born of discrimination regarding subtle principles lacks the nature of being an object for verbal designation, he says:
"The knowledge born of discrimination is liberating, has everything as its object, has everything in every way as its object, and is without succession" (Sūtra 54).
This is the fifth [section on] supernormal power (*vibhūti*).

Commentary: By the power of the aforementioned *saṃyama* alone, the knowledge that arises in the final stage is called "tāraka" (the deliverer). It is termed "tāraka" by virtue of its etymological meaning, for it delivers the yogin from the bottomless ocean of *saṃsāra*.
He states its object: "having all things as its object.
That which has all principles (*tattvas*), beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), as its object is "all-objected" (*sarvaviṣaya*).
And its nature is being entirely beyond the scope of objects;

for all principles (*tattva*) existing in every way—through all states distinguished as gross, subtle, and so forth, by those various transformations—are its objects, thus it is "entirely beyond the scope of objects" (*sarvathāviṣaya*).
He states another nature: "and it is without succession" (*akramaṃ ca*).

Because he grasps the nature of all things as they have transformed through every possible state without exception, sequence exists for him; thus the meaning is that he perceives everything simultaneously, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand, as being without sequence.
And what arises from this knowledge called *tāraka*, which is born of discrimination? He says:
"When there is equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). (Sūtra 3.55)
Commentary: Sattva and Puruṣa have been defined [in Sūtras 2.6, 2.18,
20) When there is equality of purity between these two, there is isolation (*kaivalya*);
the purity of *sattva* consists in its re-entry into its own cause through the cessation of the conceit of being the agent of all.

The purity of the *puruṣa* consists in the absence of experienced enjoyment; since this purity is common to both [the *puruṣa* and the *buddhi*], isolation (*kaivalya*) arises for the *puruṣa*, which means that liberation occurs.

Thus, having described the three internal limbs of yoga and assigned them the technical term *saṃyama*, and having established the threefold transformation (*pariṇāma*) in order to demonstrate the objects of *saṃyama*; having shown the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arising from the force of *saṃyama*—pertaining to the past, future, and present; having demonstrated the external powers, such as knowledge of the worlds, and the internal powers, such as knowledge of the body’s constitution, for the sake of attaining mastery in meditation; having explained the successive stages beginning with the conquest of the senses and the vital breaths, which lead to the victory over the elements and the *sattva* along with its states, for the attainment of the supreme human goal; and having set forth various means for the emergence of discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*), the nature of the "Star" (*tāraka*)—which occurs at the culmination of all meditative states—has been declared. It has been stated that through the attainment of that state, the *sattva* of the mind, having fulfilled its office, enters back into its own cause, whereby isolation (*kaivalya*) arises. Thus, the third chapter, the *Vibhūtipāda*, is concluded.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Vibhūtipāda, in the Pātañjala-bhāṣya-vṛtti titled Rājamārtaṇḍa, composed by Bhojadeva, the Lord of Dhārā. Thus concludes the Vibhūtipāda.
Now begins the Kaivalyapāda:
that by whose command alone liberation (kaivalya) arises without [other] means.
We praise that one, unborn, sovereign Lord, who consists of consciousness and bliss.
Now, this *Kaivalyapāda* is commenced in order to make known the nature of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) through reasoning, by means of dispelling the delusions arising from conflicting views.

In this regard, he makes this known by way of demonstrating the various causes of birth and so forth for those perfections (*siddhis*) previously mentioned: "All these perfections of mine proceed by depending merely upon birth and other such conditions as the force of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) practiced in previous lives."

Therefore, he says—[in order] to produce confidence by showing that there is no impairment of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which is to be accomplished through many births, to demonstrate the preeminence of the attainment of *samādhi*, and for the sake of its application toward isolation (*kaivalya*): "The perfections (*siddhi*) are born of birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and *samādhi*.
(Yoga Sūtra 4.1) Commentary: Some perfections have birth alone as their cause, such as the ability of birds and other creatures to travel through the air and so forth.
Or, for example, the qualities such as knowledge that arise immediately upon birth in the case of great sages like Kapila are innate (*sāṃsiddhika*);
the accomplishment through herbs is like [the power gained] from the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) such as mercury;
and the accomplishment through mantras is like the ability of some to travel through the air and so forth resulting from the recitation of mantras.
The perfection of austerity, as in the case of Viśvāmitra and others,
and the perfection of meditative absorption previously explained— these perfections arise only for those whose afflictions have been exhausted in previous births.
Therefore, just as with the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for other attainments as well, it is meditative concentration alone— practiced in previous lives— that is the cause;
mantras and so forth are merely instrumental conditions.

One might object: "Since the transformation of birth and other factors is seen in this very life in the case of Nandīśvara and others, how can it be said that samādhi practiced in another birth is the cause? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The transformation into another birth occurs through the influx of *prakṛti*."
Commentary on Kaivalya (2):
This transformation of birth and so forth that occurs for Nandīśvara and others in this very life arises from the influx of *prakṛti*;
for it is the *prakṛtis* belonging to a subsequent birth that, through their influx, produce modifications in this present birth, transforming them into the form of another species.
[Objection: But surely merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), and so forth are perceived as being produced therein;
how then can the primary elements (prakṛti) be the fulfillers [of those qualities]? To this, he says:
An external cause is not the motivator of the *prakṛtis*; rather, it serves to break through their covering, like a farmer [using water to open a canal], resulting in isolation (*kaivalya*).
The cause consists of merit (*dharma*) and so forth.
That [instrument] is not the motivator for the transformation of the *prakṛtis* into another state;
for a cause is not set in motion by its effect.
Where, then, does its operation regarding *dharma* and so forth lie? To this he says: "But from that [instrument] comes the breaking of the veil, like a farmer."

Therefore, from that very dharma being practiced, obstruction (*āvaraṇaka*)—which consists of non-dharma and so forth—is destroyed; because it is the direct opposite of that [dharma], its distinction is its cessation.
When that obstacle has been exhausted, the primordial natures (*prakṛtis*) themselves become capable of producing the desired effect.
He provides an illustration: "like a farmer."

Just as a farmer, wishing to lead water from one field to another, merely makes a breach in the barrier that obstructs the flow of water; once that is breached, the water itself undergoes a transformation by spreading forth, and he exerts no effort toward that spreading of the water— so too should it be understood regarding dharma and the other [factors].

When a yogin who has directly realized reality simultaneously desires to create many bodies for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma and for the experience of his own unsurpassed sovereignty, from what do those minds arise? To this he says:
"The transformation-minds arise from the mere state of 'I-am-ness' (asmitāmātra)."

Commentary on Kaivalya 4: The mental faculties (*citta*) belonging to the various bodies spontaneously created by the yogin emanate from the root cause, which is pure *asmitā* (ego-sense), according to his will;
like sparks from a fire, they evolve simultaneously.

Now, one might object that because many minds have different intentions, they could not perform a single action; to this he says: "Among the many, there is a single mind that acts as the motivator for their various activities."
Commentary on Kaivalya 5: Regarding the diversity of activity—that is, the multiplicity of operations—of those many minds, there is a single mind of the yogi that acts as the impeller and supervisor;
therefore, there is no state of being divided.

The meaning is this: just as one, by virtue of being the presiding agent, impels the mind, eyes, hands, and so forth within one's own body according to one's will, so too does one do so in other bodies;
for since supernatural powers (siddhis) originate from birth and other such factors, the mind that produces them is likewise of five kinds.

Therefore, he states the distinction between the mind arising from birth and so forth, and the mind arising from meditative concentration: "In that regard, that which is born of dhyāna is without latent impressions; it leads to isolation. (YS 4.25)

Commentary: That mind which is born of meditation—that is, born of *samādhi*—is "without latent disposition" (*anāśaya*) among the five [types of minds]; this means it is devoid of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma. Just as the yogi’s mind is distinct from other minds by being free from afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, he states that his karma is likewise distinct: [The verse continues: "But the karma of the yogi is not so. (YS 4.6) The meaning is that while the karma of others results in rebirth, the karma of the yogi does not. Why? Because it is performed with knowledge (*jñāna*). This is because such karma is performed with the understanding that the self (*ātman*) is distinct from the body and other [limiting adjuncts]. Furthermore, since the yogi performs actions for the sake of others, they do not result in rebirth. It is like the case of a person who has reached the end of their lifespan; even if they perform meritorious acts, those acts do not lead to further existence. Thus, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others. (YS 4.6) Furthermore, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others because it is performed with dispassion (*vairāgya*). This is because the yogi performs actions without attachment to the fruits. It is like the case of a person who has renounced all desires; even if they perform meritorious acts, they do not lead to rebirth. Therefore, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others. (YS 4.7) Moreover, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others because it is performed with non-attachment (*asaṅga*). This is because the yogi performs actions without clinging to the results. It is like the case of a person who has attained liberation (*mokṣa*); even if they perform meritorious acts, they do not lead to rebirth. Thus, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others. (YS 4.8) Additionally, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others because it is performed with equanimity (*samatva*). This is because the yogi performs actions without partiality toward the fruits. It is like the case of a person who has realized the equality of all things; even if they perform meritorious acts, they do not lead to rebirth. Therefore, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others. (YS 4.9) Finally, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others because it is performed with the realization of the truth (*tattvajñāna*). This is because the yogi performs actions with the firm conviction that the self is eternal and unchanging. It is like the case of a person who has attained the supreme knowledge; even if they perform meritorious acts, they do not lead to rebirth. Consequently, the karma of the yogi is distinct from the karma of others. (YS 4.10)
The karma of the yogi is neither-white-nor-black; for others, it is of three kinds.
[This is] the section on isolation (kaivalya).—Wholesome karma that yields auspicious results, such as sacrifice and the like, is white.
That which yields an inauspicious fruit, such as the killing of a Brahmin, is black;
that which is mixed with both is white-and-black.
Among these, white karma belongs to wise men who possess charity, austerity, Vedic study, and so forth.
The action of the Dānavas is black;
that of human beings is white and black;
but for Yogins who have renounced, it is the opposite of the threefold action, because by performing it solely with the intent of renouncing the fruit, it does not initiate any result whatsoever.
He states the fruit of this very action:
"Consequently, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (vāsanās) that are concordant with the ripening of that [action]."
Commentary on Kaivalya 8: For here, indeed, there are two kinds of karmic impressions (*karmavāsanā*): those resulting solely in memory, and those resulting in birth, lifespan, and experience.
Among these, those resulting in birth, lifespan, and experience occur over one or many births; this has already been explained previously [in Sūtra 4.1].

12–13) Those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which have already reached a definitive conclusion and whose sole fruit is memory—those very impressions, which are concordant with and correspond to the ripening (*vipāka*) of that specific action by which a particular body was commenced (whether distinguished as divine, human, animal, and so forth)—are manifested from that [ripening].

This is the meaning: when a body such as that of a deity was previously commenced by a certain action, and after an interval of hundreds of other births, upon the commencement of another body of that same kind, only those impressions whose fruit is memory and which are concordant with that [new body] become manifest.
In other worlds, memory and the other [cognitions] arise only with respect to those objects;

however, the other [objects], though they exist, remain in an unmanifest state, and in that condition, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for the production of bodies such as those of hell-beings do not become manifest.
Anticipating the objection that the causal relationship between these very latent impressions (*vāsanās*) is untenable, he says the following to establish it:
"Even for those [impressions] separated by birth, place, and time, there is immediate succession because memory and its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) are of a single form" (Kaivalya 9).

Commentary: Here, for transmigrating beings wandering through various wombs, when—after experiencing a certain womb—they attain that very same womb again after an interval of thousands of other births, then those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which had become manifest in that previously experienced womb in dependence upon such manifestors as the body and so forth, having been concealed due to the absence of such manifestors, become manifest once again upon obtaining a body or other manifestors of that same kind.
Even when separated by birth, place, and time, there is immediate succession—that is, continuity—for those [impressions] in producing their corresponding results such as memory;
why? Because memory and latent impressions (saṃskāra) are of one and the same nature.
For instance: from an action being performed, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form of a mental trace (*vāsanā*) arises within the mind-substance (*cittasattva*);

and this is the state of being a sprout for fruits such as heaven or hell, or it is the persistence of actions such as sacrifices in the form of a potency (*śakti*), or it is the capacity of the agent in the form of being an enjoyer of such objects of experience.

From the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) comes memory (*smṛti*), and from memory comes the experience of pleasure and pain; and from that experience, once again, latent impressions, memory, and so forth arise.
Thus, for one for whom memory, latent impressions, and the rest are distinct [entities], the relationship of cause and effect is difficult to establish in the absence of immediate succession.

For us, however, when experience itself becomes a latent impression, and the latent impression transforms into the form of memory, then because a single consciousness remains as the unifying synthesizer (*anusandhātṛ*), the relationship of cause and effect is not problematic.

Let it be granted that there is an immediate succession and a causal relationship among the latent impressions (*vāsanās*). However, when the very first experience occurs, one might wonder whether it is caused by a latent impression or is without cause. To dispel this doubt, he says:
"And their beginninglessness [is established] because the injunctions are eternal."

Commentary on Kaivalya 10: Regarding the beginninglessness (*anāditva*) of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it means that there exists no beginning for them; the state of having no beginning is their essential nature, which signifies that they have no origin.
Why? Because of the eternity of desire (*āśis*).

This desire, which consists of great delusion (*mahāmoha*)—the specific mental resolve (*saṃkalpaviśeṣa*) that "may these means of happiness always be mine, and may I never be separated from them"—is the cause of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); because this [desire] is eternal, its beginninglessness is the meaning.
This is what is meant: since the cause is present, who can prevent the activity of the effects, such as experience and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)?

The meaning is that the mind—which is permeated by experience and impressions, and possesses the nature of contraction and expansion—transforms into the form of this or that fruit upon obtaining the ripening (*vipāka*) that manifests it.
Anticipating the question of how their abandonment occurs given their infinity, he states the means for such abandonment:
"Because these [afflictions] are comprised of causes, fruits, supports, and objects, in the absence of these, they are absent; this is isolation. (1.11)

Commentary: The immediate cause of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is experience; the cause of that experience is passion and so forth; and the cause of those is ignorance (*avidyā*), whether directly or through a succession. The effects are the body and so forth, as well as memory and so forth.
The substratum is the intellect-substance (*buddhi-sattva*).
Whatever is the object of experience is itself the object of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, because all infinite latent impressions are subsumed within these causes, effects, bases, and objects, when these causes and so forth are absent—having been rendered like burnt seeds through the practice of knowledge and yoga—the latent impressions do not sprout, as they are rootless; they do not initiate any effect, and thus they cease to exist.

One might object: "Since the mind is observed to perish at every moment, and since the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) and their fruits do not exist simultaneously due to their relationship as cause and effect, how can there be unity when there is such difference? Anticipating this doubt, he says—in order to establish unity:
"The past and the future exist in their own nature, because of the distinction of the time-periods (*adhvan*) of phenomena (*dharma*)."
Kaivalya, verse 12, commentary: Here, the production of entities that are absolutely non-existent is not logical, because they lack any possible connection with existence;
for indeed, no connection with existence has ever been observed in the case of things such as a rabbit’s horn.
And toward an effect that is indefinable (nirupākhya), with what end in view would causes operate? For no one ever acts after perceiving a non-existent object;
nor is there a connection with non-existence, because it is contradictory even for existing things [to possess it].

The meaning is this: how can that which has acquired its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) assume a state of being indefinable (*nirupākhya*) or a state of non-existence (*abhāva*), since it does not adopt a contradictory form?

Therefore, because the non-existence of existing things is impossible and the production of non-existing things is impossible, the substratum (*dharmin*), while undergoing transformation through various attributes (*dharma*), remains eternally of one and the same nature.

The attributes, however, are established therein as belonging to the three times—that is, as being temporal—and while established in their respective time-periods (*adhvan*), they do not abandon their own essential nature.
Those [dharmas] situated in the present time-path merely possess the state of being objects of experience;

therefore, in this system, the relationship of cause and effect between dharmas themselves is established precisely through the distinction of their time-paths as past, future, and so forth, in that very form.
Consequently, it is impossible to deny that the single mind persists as the substrate (dharmin) until the point of liberation.
Regarding what the nature of these properties (dharma) and the property-possessors (dharmī) is, he says:
"They are the manifest and subtle forms, whose essence is the gunas."

Commentary on Kaivalya 13: These properties and their substrates (dharma-dharmin) which have been described are established through the distinction between the manifest and the subtle; they are the *guṇas* consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The meaning is that they have those as their essence, those as their nature, and are of the form of their transformations (*pariṇāma*).

For, by means of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—which take the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion—the persistence (*anvaya*) of these [qualities] is observed in all objective manifestations (*bhāvavyakti*), whether distinguished as external or internal.
Whatever is accompanied by something else is seen to be of the nature of its transformation,
just as jars and other objects, being accompanied by clay, are of the nature of transformations of clay.
Anticipating the objection that if these three *guṇas* are the universal root cause, how can there be the designation of a single substrate (*dharmī*), he says:
"The reality of the object is one because its transformation is one" (Kaivalya 14).

Commentary: Although there are three *guṇas*, nevertheless, because their transformation— characterized by the relationship of subordinate and predominant— is unitary (in that in some cases *sattva* is predominant, in some *rajas*, and in others *tamas*), the reality (*tattva*) of the object is said to be one,
just as [one says] "this is earth" or "this is air," and so forth.
An objection is raised: "Surely, when an object exists as something distinct from cognition, it is appropriate to say that a thing is either one or many;

but when it is consciousness itself that, through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), appears in various ways while abiding in the relationship of cause and effect, how can this [distinction] be asserted? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Because of the difference in the minds despite the identity of the object, the path of these two is distinct; this is the function [of the sūtra]. "The distinct path of those two"—namely, knowledge and the object—means a distinct way, or in other words, a distinct region.
How is it that, despite the identity of the object, there is a difference in the mind? That is to say,
when a single object such as a woman is perceived, a difference in the minds of various perceivers is observed in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

For instance, when a single woman endowed with beauty and grace is perceived, pleasure arises in one who possesses passion, hatred in a rival wife, and disgust in a wandering mendicant or the like; since diverse states of mind arise toward a single object, how can the object be the effect of the mind? If it were the effect of a single mind, the object would appear only in that single form. Furthermore, if the object were the effect of the mind, then while the mind to which that object belongs is preoccupied with another object, that object would become nothing at all. If you say, "Let it be so," [we reply: no.
How could that very same object be perceived by many others, and yet it is so perceived? Therefore, it is not the effect of the mind.
Furthermore, if that object were produced simultaneously by many, then there would be a distinction between an object created by many and one created by a single person.
But when difference is not admitted, then, given a difference in causes, if there were an absence of difference in the effect, the world would be either causeless or of a single uniform nature.

This is what is meant: even though the causes are distinct, if there were no distinction in the effect, then the entire world—produced from various kinds of causes—would be of a single uniform nature because it would not follow the diversity of its causes; or else, being independent [of those causes], it would be causeless.
If this is so, how is it that by means of that mind, which consists of the three *guṇas*, cognitions composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion are produced for a single knower?
Do not say so;
for as the object is composed of the three *guṇas*, so too is the mind composed of the three *guṇas*.
When the appearance of an object arises, factors such as merit (*dharma*) serve as its auxiliary causes;
through the power of their emergence or suppression, the mind is occasionally manifested in various forms.
Thus, for example, when a woman is present, the mind of a lustful man—assisted by merit and transforming with *sattva* as its dominant quality—becomes composed of pleasure.
That very same [cognition], when accompanied by demerit (*adharma*) and dominated by *rajas*, takes the form of suffering for a co-wife;
when it transforms through intense accompaniment by demerit and is dominated by *tamas*, it becomes filled with delusion for an angry co-wife.
Therefore, the object of apprehension exists as distinct from consciousness.
Thus, because identity between consciousness and its object is contradictory, there can be no relationship of cause and effect;
for even if the cause were non-different, it would follow that the effects must also be non-different. Therefore, it is established that the object is distinct from cognition.

If this is so—that cognition, because it is illuminating, has the nature of a grasper, and the object, because it is illuminated, has the nature of the grasped—then why does it not simultaneously grasp and remember all objects?
To dispel this doubt, he says:
"Because the mind depends on the coloring by that [object], an entity is known or unknown."
Kaivalya, verse 16, commentary: Due to the coloring by that object—that is, through the imparting of its form—the external thing becomes known or unknown within the mind.
The meaning of this is as follows: every entity depends upon the mind as a causal complex for its own manifestation.
Furthermore, the cognition of blue and so forth, as it arises, depends upon the coloring by the object (arthoparāga) transmitted through the channel of the sense organ as its auxiliary cause;
for since there is no connection with a distinct object, that object cannot otherwise be apprehended.
Consequently, that very object by which the coloring of its own nature (svarūpoparāga) has been produced is led by that cognition to a state of being fit for conventional usage (vyavahārayogyatā).
Therefore, that object is said to be "known" by which its form is presented;
yet that [object] for which no such form is presented is not treated as being known.

Furthermore, when an experienced object—such as similarity and the like—acts as a cooperative cause by awakening a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it is precisely upon that object that memory arises. Thus, there is no contradiction in the fact that there is neither cognition nor memory in every case.

If this is so, one might raise the objection that even the cognizing person (*puruṣa*), at the time he perceives blue, would—since the mental being (*cittasattva*) possessing yellow and other qualities is also occasionally of the nature of a grasper—undergo transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) in the grasping of forms. To dispel this doubt, he says:
"The fluctuations of the mind are always known, because their Lord, the *puruṣa*, is unchanging."

Commentary on Kaivalya 17: These fluctuations of the mind, which take the form of valid cognition, error, and so forth, are always known at all times by the Puruṣa who is their master and the perceiver of them;
this is because, being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), he is unchanging, meaning he lacks the quality of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

If that [Puruṣa] were subject to transformation (*pariṇāmī*), then because transformation occurs only occasionally, the constant knownness of those mental fluctuations would not be possible. This is the meaning: since the Puruṣa, whose nature is consciousness, remains eternally established as the presiding witness, his internal organ—pure *sattva*—also exists eternally. Whatever object colors it, there is always the presence of the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā-saṃkrānti*) upon that [internal organ] corresponding to such an object; and this being present, its status as a knower is established. Thus, there is never any suspicion of its being subject to transformation. 17

Now, one might object: "If it is the mind alone that illuminates due to its excellence as a sentient being, then, because it has the nature of illuminating both itself and objects, it illuminates itself and the object; by that much alone, the completion of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is achieved.
What is the use of another grasper? To dispel this doubt, he says:
"It does not have its own appearance, because it is an object of perception."
Commentary on Kaivalya 18: That mind is not self-luminous—that is, it does not illuminate itself—but is rather known by the Puruṣa;
why is this so?
Because it is an object of sight;
for whatever is indeed an object of sight is known by a seer, as in the case of a jar or similar objects, and the mind is an object of sight; therefore, it does not manifest itself.
But is it not the case that this reason is non-different from the probandum,
since the very visibility of the mind is unestablished?
Furthermore, functional activities in the form of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful are observed through the medium of one's own awareness of the intellect (*buddhi*).
For instance, such cognitions as "I am angry," "I am afraid," or "I have passion for this" would not be possible if there were no awareness of the intellect. To dispel this doubt, he says:
"And at one and the same time, there is no apprehension of both."

Commentary on Kaivalya 19: The cognition of an object is the production of its fitness for practical usage through the determination "this is it," such as "this object is a cause of pleasure" or "this object is a cause of pain."
The production of the intellect (*buddhi*)— which consists of consciousness— in such forms as "I" and as pleasure or pain, thereby rendering it fit for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*),
and this twofold activity of such a kind cannot be performed simultaneously at the time of the direct perception of an object, because of their mutual contradiction; indeed,
there is no possibility of two contradictory activities occurring at once.
Therefore, because it is impossible to ascertain both the nature [of the cognition] and the object simultaneously at one time, the mind is not self-illuminating;

rather, since the two results produced by these two kinds of operations are not experienced [simultaneously], the result resides only in the object and not in itself, because the mind experiences itself only through its own state of being directed outwardly—this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "Let there be no self-apprehension of cognition; it will be apprehended by another cognition. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If cognition were visible to another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions and a confusion of memories" (Kaivalya 20).

Commentary: For if one cognition were to be known by another cognition, that [second] cognition, being itself unperceived, would be incapable of illuminating the other cognition; thus, another cognition would have to be postulated as its grasper, and yet another for that one as well, resulting in an infinite regress. Consequently, the apprehension of an object by another person would never occur, for an object does not become apprehended when the apprehension itself remains unapprehended.

Furthermore, a confusion of memories would result: when a cognition arises regarding either form or taste, because infinite cognitions grasping those objects arise, and when many simultaneous memories are produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by those cognitions, then—due to the lack of finality in cognition and the simultaneous arising of many cognitions and memories—it would be impossible to know for which object this particular memory has arisen; thus, there would be a confusion of memories, such that one could not distinguish, "This is a memory of form," or "This is a memory of taste. (20)

Now, one might object: "If consciousness (*buddhi*) lacks self-luminosity and is not perceived by another consciousness, how can this empirical activity consisting of the perception of objects occur? Anticipating this doubt, he states his own established doctrine:
"The perception of one's own consciousness occurs when consciousness, which is non-transitive, assumes the form of that [object]" (Kaivalya 21).
Commentary: The Puruṣa is consciousness because its nature is consciousness (*cit*). It is "non-transitive" (*apratisaṃkramā*);
that is to say, it is so called because there is no transference (*pratisaṃkrama*)—meaning movement elsewhere—of it, which is to say, it is not mixed with anything else.
Just as the qualities (guṇas) migrate into the principal quality during a transformation characterized by the relationship of part and whole, thereby seemingly assuming its form;

or just as atoms in the world, when spreading out, take on the form of the object—so it is not with the power of consciousness (citiśakti), because it remains firmly established through its eternal uniformity.

Therefore, when the intellect (*buddhi*) assumes the form of that [object] in its proximity, it arises as if conscious; and when the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), reflected in the modification of the intellect, is perceived as being distinguished by that mental modification, then there occurs the perception—that is, the self-awareness—of the intellect itself. This is the meaning. (21) Thus, he states that the mind, being self-cognized in this manner, will be capable of sustaining all worldly transactions through its capacity to apprehend everything: [The verse follows: "The mind, though insentient, appears as if sentient due to the proximity of the conscious principle; and the conscious principle, though unchanging, appears as if changing due to the proximity of the mind. The mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, is the knower of all objects. (Yoga Sūtra 1.4) Commentary: The seer is the *puruṣa*; colored by him—that is, through his proximity—it attains, as it were, his own form. When it becomes colored by the seen, colored by the object—meaning it undergoes a transformation into the form of the perceived object—then that very mind becomes capable of grasping all objects.

Just as a stainless crystal, mirror, or similar object alone is capable of receiving a reflection, so too the *sattva* quality, when unoverpowered by *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes capable of receiving the shadow of consciousness due to its purity; however, *rajas* and *tamas* are not so capable because of their impurity.

In that state, *sattva*—in which *rajas* and *tamas* have become subordinated (*aṅgibhūta*)—remains in a single, constant form like the flame of a steady lamp. Due to its capacity to receive the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*), it persists until liberation is attained.

Just as the movement of iron manifests when a magnet is in proximity, so too does consciousness (*caitanya*), which is to be manifested, manifest within *sattva* when the Puruṣa, whose nature is consciousness, is in proximity.
For this very reason, in this system there are two powers of consciousness: the eternally manifest (*nityoditā*) and the manifested (*abhivyaṅgyā*).
The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is eternally manifest; however, through proximity to the *puruṣa*, the *sattva*—whose consciousness is manifested—becomes the object of manifestation.

Because it is extremely proximate to the *puruṣa*, this manifested power of consciousness becomes the internal organ (*antaraṅga*) for the *puruṣa* and attains the state of being an object of experience (*bhogyatā*).

This very [state] is designated by the Sāṃkhyas, who propound the doctrine of the peaceful Brahman, as that which is presided over by the *puruṣa* (the Supreme Self) and which, in accordance with one's karma, experiences pleasure and pain.

However, because not even a single quality (*guṇa*) is ever predominant, and since at any given time one [quality] may serve as the principal (*aṅgin*), the triad of qualities (*triguṇa*) undergoes transformation every moment. Being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and being impure, that [Prakṛti] brings about the state of being perceivable by means of projecting its own form onto the pure *sattva*—which is in accordance with [the individual's] karma. That very first pure *sattva* of the mind (*cittasattva*), having received the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) from elsewhere, experiences enjoyment in the form of pleasure and pain; although it lacks actual consciousness, it becomes conscious through the power of the reflection of consciousness, as the object-form assumed by the mind is presented to it.

Because that very experience is in such close proximity [to the Self], and because of the failure to perceive their distinction, it is designated as "experience" even for the Puruṣa, though he is not the actual experiencer.
With this very intention, Vindhyavāsin stated: "The suffering of the *sattva* itself is the suffering of the Puruṣa.

Likewise, it is said elsewhere: "In the case of a reflection, the arising of a shadow resembling the shadow of the object being reflected is what is expressed by the term 'reflection' (*pratibimba*)."
Thus, even in the case of a sentient being, the manifestation of consciousness resembling the reflection of a human consciousness is the meaning of the term "transference" (*pratisaṅkrānti*);
for is it not observed that what is called a "reflection" occurs when a pure object with a determinate transformation is reflected in something pure, as a face in a mirror?
"How can reflection be possible for a Puruṣa who is absolutely pure, all-pervading, and unchanging, upon an impure Sattva, given that [Sattva] is not absolutely pure as the Puruṣa is?
It is said in reply: This was asserted by you because you do not understand the true nature of reflection;
the very manifestation of the power of consciousness (cicchakti)—which resides in Sattva and is to be manifested—due to its proximity to the Puruṣa, is what is called "reflection."
Whatever nature the power of consciousness (cicchakti) residing in the Puruṣa possesses, its reflection likewise manifests here [in Prakṛti].
As for the objection raised—that since the Puruṣa is absolutely pure, how can it be reflected in the impure Sattva?—that too is inconclusive;
for even in substances like water, which are inferior in purity, the sun and other luminaries are observed to be reflected.

As for what was said—that there is no reflection (*pratisaṃkrānti*) of that which is undivided—that too is incorrect, because even the all-pervading ether (*ākāśa*) is seen to be reflected in mirrors and the like.
This being so, there is no logical inconsistency in the perception of reflections.

Now, it has been stated that when the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is to be manifested through proximity to the *puruṣa*, undergoes a transfer of external forms within the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is itself a transformation of the *sāttvika* quality—the *puruṣa* experiences enjoyment (*bhoga*) in the form of pleasure and pain; however, that is untenable.

How can that very same mental essence (*cittasattva*) exist when primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has not undergone transformation, and for what purpose does its transformation occur? If it is argued that she must accomplish the experience of objects for the sake of the *puruṣa*,
then her transformation is indeed justified by the necessity of fulfilling the *puruṣa*’s purpose.
And that is untenable,

because the very notion of "the duty to act for the sake of human ends" is untenable; for the determination that "I must perform such-and-such a human end" is what is called the duty to act for the sake of human ends.
How can such a volitional determination (*adhyavasāya*) arise from insentient *prakṛti* at the very outset? If such a determination exists, how can it be called insentient?
To this it is replied: there exists an innate pair of powers within the two-fold transformation characterized by the forward (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) orders.
That very capacity for performing the purpose of the Puruṣa is now described; and that power is indeed innate to Prakṛti, even though she is insentient.
In this regard, her transformation from Mahat down to the gross elements is the "forward" (anuloma) evolution, occurring through her outward orientation.
Furthermore, by way of re-entering its own causes, the transformation culminates in *asmitā* (egoism) in reverse order.
In this manner, upon the completion of the Spirit’s experience and the exhaustion of the two innate powers, *prakṛti*, having accomplished its purpose, does not initiate further transformation.
And regarding such a fulfillment of the Spirit’s aim, there is no logical inconsistency even for the insentient *prakṛti*.
[Objection: If such a power exists as innate to *pradhāna* itself, then for what purpose is effort made by those seeking liberation for the sake of liberation?
Furthermore, if liberation were not to be sought, the treatise that teaches it would be purposeless.

[Reply: It is said: When this beginningless relationship between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, characterized by the roles of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, exists, and when *prakṛti*—whose consciousness is unmanifest—experiences suffering due to the conceit of agency, there certainly arises the resolve: "How might this absolute cessation of suffering be mine?"
Therefore, there is indeed a dependence upon the instruction of a Teacher who teaches the means for the cessation of suffering;
for the *buddhisattva* (the faculty of discernment) of *pradhāna*, which corresponds exactly to such karma, is the very object of the Teacher’s instruction.
Even in other systems of philosophy, it is precisely this kind of nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) that is addressed by the Teacher.
And he, while striving for liberation, attains the fruit called liberation by depending upon such instruction from the Teacher as a cooperative cause;
for all effects indeed come into being when their causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present.

By means of a reverse-order transformation (*pratilomapariṇāma*), it is established through valid cognition that for this effect called liberation—which is to be produced—such a causal totality alone is required, since no other mode is possible.
Therefore, how could it exist without her?

Thus, this is established: the *buddhi-sattva*, reflecting the shadow of consciousness (*cit-chāyā*) through the coloring (*uparāga*) of the object that has been transferred to it, carries out the entire course of worldly life by means of the determination of objects.
Those who, perceiving the mind as being of such a nature, are deluded and assert that "the mind is self-cognizing" and "the world is mind-only," are thereby enlightened.

Now, one might object: "If the accomplishment of all worldly transactions proceeds from such a mind alone, how can a seer devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be accepted? Anticipating this doubt, he states the means of valid cognition for the seer: "Although that [mind] is variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it exists for the sake of another because it functions through aggregation."

Commentary on Kaivalya 23: Even though that very mind is variegated—meaning manifold—due to latent impressions (*vāsanās*) that are impossible to enumerate, it exists for the sake of another; that is, it accomplishes the purpose of the other, namely the master or enjoyer, which consists of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).
Why is this so?

Because they act collectively— that is, because they perform purposeful activity by acting together, combining, and assembling— whatever performs purposeful activity through collective action is seen to be for the sake of another,
such as a bed, a seat, and so forth.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas possess the characteristics of the mind and undergo transformation; they act in combination and therefore exist for the sake of another.
That "other" is the Puruṣa.

Now, one might object: based on the force of the observed example of how beds, seats, and the like—which have a body as their "other"—exist for the sake of another, it follows that the "other" established must be of that same kind [i.e., possessing a body].

Furthermore, since you intend a "supreme" [agent] (*para*) who is of an uncomposite nature (*asaṃhata-rūpa*), this reason—which establishes the opposite of that—is said to be one that subverts what is desired (*iṣṭavighātaka*).

Although the pervasion (*vyāpti*) was grasped in a general sense merely as "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*), nevertheless, by considering the subject (*dharmin*) which possesses properties distinct from those such as existence (*sattva*), a supreme enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is established as being distinct from them.
Just as when fire is inferred from smoke on a mountain peak covered with sandalwood, the fire perceived is understood to be distinct from other fires and produced specifically from sandalwood.

In the same way here as well, when it is inferred that the object of experience—known as "sentient being" (*sattva*) and characterized by distinct qualities—is for the sake of another, there is established a corresponding experiencer and controller: the Supreme, whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and who is uncomposite.

And if his supremacy is understood as being the most excellent of all, nevertheless, the body is superior to objects of the *tamas* quality because it is the substratum of the organs which are of the nature of light;
and the organs are superior even to that [body].
Even more excellent than that is *sattva*, which has the nature of illumination;
and that which is its illuminator, being distinct from the illuminated, is itself of the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Therefore, how could it possess the quality of being a composite?

Now, he begins with ten aphorisms to determine the fruit of the treatise, which is isolation (*kaivalya*): "For one who perceives the distinction, there is the cessation of the cultivation of self-identity; this is isolation" (YS 1.24).

Commentary: Thus, when the distinctness of the *sattva* (the intellect) and the *puruṣa* (the self) has been established, for one who perceives their specific difference—namely, in the form "this [self] is different from that [intellect]"—the cultivation of the notion of self-identity within the mind of that *sattva*, whose true nature as consciousness has been realized, ceases;
that is, the conceit that "the mind alone is the agent, the knower, and the enjoyer" ceases.
He explains what happens when that [discriminative discernment] exists:
"At that time, the mind flows toward discrimination and inclines toward isolation" (Kaivalya Sūtra 1.25).

Commentary: That mind which was previously inclined toward ignorance, extroverted, and having the enjoyment of sense-objects as its fruit, now becomes inclined toward discrimination, directed inward along the path of discrimination, leaning toward isolation (*kaivalya*), and commencing toward isolation. And regarding those obstacles that arise in this mind flowing toward discrimination, he states the means for their abandonment by way of explaining their causes: 25. *tadvairāgyādapi doṣabījakṣaye kaivalyam* // YS 3.50 When even through detachment from that [mind], the seeds of the defects are destroyed, there is isolation. (YS 3.50) The word "even" (*api*) implies that isolation occurs not only through the practice of yoga, but also through detachment from that mind. What is meant by "detachment"? It is the absence of passion for objects perceived through the senses, whether they be seen, heard, or inferred, whether they be past, present, or future, whether they be subtle, concealed, or distant; it is the absence of passion for all objects whatsoever. This is detachment. What is the seed of the defects? It is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the defects. From that [seed], the defects arise again. When that seed of the defects is destroyed by the power of detachment, the mind ceases to function. When it ceases to function, the self remains in its own nature, free from both merit and demerit, and thus attains isolation. This is called isolation. Furthermore, when the mind flows toward discrimination, whatever obstacles manifest, he describes the means for abandoning them by way of demonstrating their causes: *tasya saptadhā prāntabhūmiḥ prajñā* // YS 3.51 His discernment (*prajñā*) has seven stages of culmination. (YS 3.51) The discernment of one whose mind flows toward discrimination reaches a state of culmination in seven ways. What are these seven? They are: the discernment of the distinction between the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the knower (*jña*); the discernment of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the purpose of the *guṇas*; the discernment of the distinction between the *sādhana* (means) and the *siddhi* (attainment); the discernment of the distinction between the various forms of *siddhi*; the discernment of the distinction between the various forms of contentment (*tuṣṭi*); the discernment of the distinction between the various forms of power (*aiśvarya*); and the discernment of the distinction between the *kaivalya* of the *guṇas* and the *kaivalya* of the self. These are the seven stages of culmination of discernment. Among these, the discernment of the distinction between the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower is the primary one. The others are secondary. Among these, the discernment of the distinction between the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower is as follows: The manifest is composed of the three *guṇas*. It is objective, common to all, non-intelligent, and productive. The unmanifest is the opposite of that. The knower is the Spirit (*puruṣa*), who is consciousness alone. This is the discernment of the distinction between the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower. The discernment of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the purpose of the *guṇas* is as follows: The *guṇas* consist of the three—sattva, rajas, and tamas. Their purpose is experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). This is the discernment of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the purpose of the *guṇas*. The discernment of the distinction between the *sādhana* and the *siddhi* is as follows: The *sādhana* consists of the eight limbs of yoga. The *siddhi* is the attainment of the fruits thereof. This is the discernment of the distinction between the *sādhana* and the *siddhi*. The discernment of the distinction between the various forms of *siddhi* is as follows: The *siddhis* are the eight great powers, such as becoming minute (*aṇiman*). This is the discernment of the distinction between the various forms of *siddhi*. The discernment of the distinction between the various forms of contentment is as follows: Contentment is of nine kinds, beginning with the "inner lack" (*ādhyātmika*). This is the discernment of the distinction between the various forms of contentment. The discernment of the distinction between the various forms of power is as follows: Power is of eight kinds, such as the power to become minute. This is the discernment of the distinction between the various forms of power. The discernment of the distinction between the *kaivalya* of the *guṇas* and the *kaivalya* of the self is as follows: The *kaivalya* of the *guṇas* is their return to their own cause after having fulfilled their purpose. The *kaivalya* of the self is its abiding in its own nature, free from the *guṇas*. This is the discernment of the distinction between the *kaivalya* of the *guṇas* and the *kaivalya* of the self. Among these, the discernment of the distinction between the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower is the primary one. The others are secondary. For what reason? Because the discernment of the distinction between the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower is the means for the attainment of all other discernments. Therefore, it is the primary one. The others are secondary because they are subordinate to it. Thus ends the third chapter of the *Yogasūtrabhāṣyavivaraṇa*, titled "Kaivalyapāda. [End of Chapter 3] [Chapter 4 begins: Now, the fourth chapter, "Kaivalyapāda," is commenced. In this chapter, the nature of isolation (*kaivalya*) will be explained. Isolation is the state of the self remaining in its own nature, free from the *guṇas*. To explain that, he first states the means for its attainment: *janmauṣadhimantratapaḥsamādhijāḥ siddhayaḥ* // YS 4.1 The supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are born of birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and samādhi. (YS 4.1) The powers are of five kinds: those born of birth, those born of herbs, those born of mantras, those born of austerity, and those born of samādhi. Among these, the powers born of birth are, for example, the powers possessed by the gods, Gandharvas, and others. The powers born of herbs are, for example, the power to become invisible attained by using the herb *rasāñjana*. The powers born of mantras are, for example, the power to enter another's body attained by reciting specific mantras. The powers born of austerity are, for example, the power to reach the sun attained by the austerity of fasting. The powers born of samādhi are, for example, the power to become minute attained through the practice of *samādhi*. Among these, the powers born of samādhi are the most excellent. Why? Because they are free from all defects. The others are inferior because they are accompanied by defects. Thus, the powers born of samādhi are the most excellent. (YS 4.2) The transformation of the body into another species occurs because of the influx of the *prakṛtis*. What is meant by "influx"? It is the arrival of the *prakṛtis* into the channels of the body. Through that influx, the body transforms into another species. For example, a human body may transform into the body of a tiger or a wolf. From the *samādhi* known as the Cloud of Virtue. What is the Cloud of Virtue?
In the gaps [of that state], other cognitions arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); this is the function [of the *kaivalya* stage].—

For one established in that *samādhi*, during the gaps or intervals, those other cognitions which take the form of emergence (*vyutthāna*)— namely, knowledges such as "I" and "mine"— manifest even though they are derived from previously existing latent impressions born of the experience of emergence, even as those impressions are being exhausted.
It has been stated that their abandonment must be accomplished by means of the destruction of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
and since the means for such abandonment has already been explained, he says:

Their abandonment is stated to be like that of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Commentary: Just as the abandonment of the afflictions, such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest, was previously explained, [so too is the abandonment of these]. (2)

10–11) Likewise, one should act toward the formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*) in such a way that, scorched by the fire of knowledge and resembling burnt seeds, they no longer find growth in the soil of the mind; so too with the formative predispositions.
And when concentration has thus become stabilized through the non-arising of other intervening conditions, he describes the means by which a yogi attains the culmination of such concentration:
"For one who is not even indifferent toward *prasaṅkhyāna*, there arises from discriminative discernment in every respect the *dharmamegha* concentration, which is isolation. (YS 4.29)
Commentary: Prasaṃkhyāna is the discernment of the distinct natures of as many principles (tattvas) as there are, arranged in their proper sequence.

When that [discernment] exists, for one who is non-indolent and free from desire for results, because no other cognitions arise and because discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti) has reached its ultimate state, the "Cloud of Dharma" (dharmamegha) samādhi occurs.
It is called the "Cloud of Dharma" because it rains down—that is, pours forth—the preeminent, neither-white-nor-black dharma which accomplishes the supreme goal of man (paramapuruṣārtha).
By this, it is established that only the preeminent dharma is the cause of knowledge.
Therefore, he states what arises from that "Cloud of Dharma" (dharmamegha):
Thence follows the cessation of afflictions and karma, which is isolation (kaivalya).

Regarding this state: through the arising of knowledge, there occurs the cessation of the afflictions—beginning with ignorance and ending with the clinging to life—and of the three types of karma, such as the white and so forth, by means of the cessation of each preceding cause.
When those [obstacles] have ceased, what happens? He says:
"Then, because the knowledge that is free from all the stains of obscuration is infinite, the knowable is small."

Commentary on Kaivalya 30: Those by which the mind is covered are the "obscuring factors" (āvaraṇa), namely the afflictions (kleśa); these are themselves the impurities. For knowledge that is free from them—that is, devoid of them—being like the sky, because of its infinity and lack of limitation, the knowable becomes small, merely an object of counting.
The meaning is that one knows all that is knowable without any difficulty whatsoever.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Consequently, for those whose purpose has been accomplished, there is a cessation of the sequence of the transformation of the guṇas."

Commentary on Kaivalya (31): Those whose purpose— the aim of the Puruṣa characterized by experience and liberation— has been accomplished or brought to completion are the "perfected" Guṇas, namely Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas.

The transformation of these [guṇas], characterized by their state of persistence, consists in the relationship of primary and subordinate factors (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) proceeding both forwardly and backwardly until the fulfillment of the purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha).
The "completion" of that sequence which is about to be described means its finality, the sense being that there is no further recurrence.
He states the definition of the aforementioned succession (krama):
Succession is that which has moments as its counter-correlate and is to be apprehended through the final limit of transformation.
Kaivalya, 32.

Vṛtti: A moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the smallest unit of time. That which is its opposite—a transformation distinct from a single moment, discernible only at its final limit (*apāranta*), and which is grasped only subsequently by a synthesizing cognition (*saṃkalana-buddhi*) regarding moments already experienced—is called the sequence (*krama*) of moments.
Indeed, a sequence cannot be known among moments that have not been experienced.
Now he states the unique nature of isolation (*kaivalya*), which is the fruit [of yoga]:
"Isolation is the re-absorption of the *guṇas* that are devoid of the purpose of the *puruṣa*, or it is the establishment of the power of consciousness in its own nature."
Isolation (kaivalya) 33:

The commentary states—when the purposes of the person (*puruṣārtha*), characterized by experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), have been completed, there is a re-absorption (*pratiprasava*) of the *guṇas*. This is the non-arising of transformations at the conclusion of the reverse-order evolution; or rather, when the conformity of the cognitive faculty (*citiśakti*) with its modifications has ceased, its abiding in its own essential nature—that is called isolation.

Thus, having described the perfection of *samādhi*—which is distinct from other perfections and is the root of all perfections—and having established that the cause of the specific perfection characterized by the transformation of one birth into another is simply the filling of *prakṛti*; having demonstrated that merit (*dharma*) and the other factors have efficacy only in the mere removal of obstacles; having stated that the emanated minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) arise from pure egoism (*asmitāmātra*); having shown that the yogi’s mind alone is the presiding controller of those [emanated minds]; having described the distinction of the yogi’s mind from other minds; having established the non-worldly nature of its actions; having demonstrated the capacity for the manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are concordant with their fruition through the demonstration of the identity of cause and effect, thereby establishing the immediate succession of even distant impressions; having shown how to abandon those impressions despite their infinity by means of causes, effects, and so forth; having established the existence of *dharmas* in the past and other time-periods; having refuted the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*) and established the doctrine of the possession of forms (*sākāravāda*); having stated the knower-ship of the *puruṣa*; having established the accomplishment of all worldly transactions through the medium of the mind; having presented the proof for the existence of the *puruṣa*; and having, by means of ten aphorisms, sequentially explained the relevant matters for the determination of isolation (*kaivalya*), and having further demonstrated that this very isolation is what is meant in other treatises—the nature of isolation has been determined, and thus the *Kaivalyapāda* is concluded.
