It is not only in our own system that the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is of such a nature as pure consciousness (*cidrūpa*) in the state of isolation (*kaivalya*); rather, even when examined within other systems of philosophy, it remains established in this very form.

For instance: in the state of *saṃsāra*, the self (*ātman*) is perceived as consisting of agency, enjoyership, and the synthesis of [past and future experiences]. Otherwise, if this single knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) were not of such a nature, then—given that moments of cognition themselves are devoid of a synthesizer of preceding and succeeding states and constitute the self—the fixed connection between action and its fruit would not exist, and there would follow the fallacy of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).

If the agency of experiencing belonged only to that very [moment] by which the action taught in the scripture was performed, then the engagement of everyone toward the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful would be impossible; for all worldly activity, characterized by rejection and acquisition, occurs only through a continuous synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and because moments of cognition are distinct from one another, they lack such synthesis. Since no worldly activity could be established in the absence of that synthesis, it is therefore established that the Self is that which is the agent, the experiencer, and the synthesizer.

In the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), however, because all conventional designations characterized by the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) have ceased to exist, only pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) remains for it. And that consciousness is established as being merely the act of cognizing (*citimātratva*), not through self-perception (*ātmasaṃvedana*). This is because the very nature of consciousness (*cite rūpa*) consists solely in its capacity to apprehend objects, not in its capacity to grasp itself. For instance, when an object is apprehended by consciousness, it is apprehended as "this"; when its own form is apprehended, it is apprehended as "I. It is not possible, however, to simultaneously perform two mutually contradictory operations characterized by being outward-turned (*bahir-mukhatā*) and inward-turned (*antar-mukhatā*).
Therefore, since it is impossible to perform two activities simultaneously, [the Self] remains as pure consciousness alone;
thus, in the state of liberation, when the *guṇas* have ceased their functions, it is logical that the Self abides in the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone.

However, in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), all such agency, enjoyership, and the capacity for synthetic reflection (*anusandhātṛtva*) are possible for one who is of this very nature.

For instance: this beginningless, innate connection of this [Puruṣa] with Prakṛti, characterized by the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed, is rooted in the lack of discriminative discernment (avivekakhyāti).

When this exists—that is, when there is the conjunction of the two powers consisting of the capacity for the Puruṣa’s purposeful activity—then, upon that conjunction, there occurs the Puruṣa’s state of being the presiding director and the capacity of the *buddhi-sattva* to receive the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*), as well as the capacity of the *buddhi-sattva* to grasp the reflected consciousness. And from this very fact—the determination of agency and enjoyership belonging to the *buddhi* which is embraced by consciousness—all worldly transaction preceded by synthesis is accomplished. What need is there for other trivial fictions and idle disputations?
If, however, an ultimate agency and so forth of the self were admitted apart from such a path [of realization], then it would follow that it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).
And due to being subject to transformation, it would be impermanent; and if it were impermanent, its very nature as a self (*ātmatva*) would not exist.
For it is impossible for mutually contradictory states to be experienced by a single entity in a single moment in a single form.

For instance: in that state in which there arises happiness inherent in the self (*ātman*), it is the experiencer of that [happiness], but not in that very same state the experiencer of suffering. Therefore, because the states are distinct, the possessor of those states—who is non-different from them—must also be manifold; and because of this manifoldness, due to its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), it cannot be the self.
Nor is there permanence;

for this very reason, the Sāṃkhyas, who propound the doctrine of the peaceful Brahman, maintain that the self always possesses a single form, both during the state of worldly existence and in the state of liberation.
However, as for those Vedāntins who consider the self's nature of consciousness and bliss to be liberation, their position is not tenable.

To explain: since bliss (*ānanda*) has the nature of happiness (*sukha*), and since happiness always appears only as being perceived, its state of being perceived cannot be established apart from the act of perception. Thus, by the admission of both the perceived object and the perception, non-duality (*advaita*) is lost.
If it were argued that bliss is indeed of the very nature of perception itself, that would be untenable due to the imposition of contradictory attributes;
for perception and the perceived object cannot possibly be one and the same.

Furthermore, the proponents of non-dualism (advaitavādins) accept that the self is twofold, distinguished as the *karmātman* and the *paramātman*. Now, if the Supreme Self were to possess the status of being an enjoyer of pleasure and pain in the very same form as the *karmātman*, then, like the *karmātman*, the Supreme Self would necessarily be subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) and would have ignorance (*avidyā*) as its inherent nature.

On the other hand, if it is not His direct state of being an enjoyer, but rather He accepts what is offered by that [empirical self] through His role as an indifferent presiding witness (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), then one has entered into our own philosophical system.
Furthermore, the nature of bliss has already been refuted;

moreover, if [the self] were of the nature of ignorance, it would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), and thus who among those whose essence is karma would have the qualification for the scriptures?
Certainly not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because it is eternally liberated.
Nor can karma have ignorance as its intrinsic nature, because [ignorance] is not its essence;
consequently, it would follow that all the scriptures are rendered useless.
Furthermore, if the world is accepted as being composed of ignorance, one must investigate whose ignorance it is.

Since the Supreme Self is eternally liberated and of the nature of pure knowledge, and since even the individual self (karmātman) is in the ultimate sense devoid of intrinsic nature—thus resembling a hare's horn—how can there be a connection with ignorance? Now, it might be argued as follows: [nama]...
This indeed is the very nature of ignorance— that it is not to be investigated;
for that which, through investigation, becomes pure like mist touched by the sun, is called "ignorance"— it is not so.
Whatever entity performs any action must necessarily be described as either different or non-different from something else;
and since it must be admitted that ignorance (avidyā) is the agent of the effect characterized by saṃsāra,
if its indefinability (anirvācyatva) were asserted despite this fact, then nothing at all could be definable, and it would follow that even Brahman is indefinable.
Therefore, no form of the self other than that of being a presiding agent is tenable;
and this presiding agency is nothing other than the nature of consciousness (cidrūpatva), because no property distinct from that can be established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Even those such as the Naiyāyikas who claim that the self is conscious due to its conjunction with consciousness (cetanā)—for them, too, that consciousness arises from the contact of the self with the mind (manas).

For instance: those qualities such as desire, cognition, and effort arise for that [self] during the state of worldly activity (*vyavahāradaśā*) from the conjunction of the self and the mind; and by means of these very qualities, it is designated as the knower, the agent, and the enjoyer.
However, in the state of liberation (*mokṣadaśā*), upon the cessation of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), there is also the cessation of the defects rooted therein.

The total destruction of those specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), such as intellect and the rest, and the self’s abiding in its own essential nature alone—this is what they accept. This position of theirs is untenable.

Since qualities such as eternality and omnipresence belong to ether (*ākāśa*) and other elements as well in that state, the nature of the Self as consisting of consciousness (*cid-rūpatva*) must necessarily be accepted as distinct from them;
if it is argued that this refers to the connection with a genus (*jāti*) distinct from "Selfhood" (*ātmatva*), we say no.
Since the conjunction with those [material] universals (jāti) is possible for everything,
one must necessarily admit that the Self is distinct from these universals;
its status as a presiding controller is only logically tenable through its nature as consciousness, and not otherwise.
Even for those Mīmāṃsakas who accept the self as having the nature of both agent and object, their position is not tenable;
for their proposition is that the self is apprehended by the notion of "I," and in that notion of "I," both agency and objectivity belong to the self alone.
Moreover, this is not tenable because of its inherent contradiction: agency, the state of being a knower, and the state of being an object, as well as knowability—
this superimposition of contradictory attributes upon a single entity cannot occur simultaneously.
That which is superposed with contradictory properties is not one, just as existence and non-existence are contradictory;
and agency and objecthood are contradictory.
If it is argued: "There is no contradiction between agency and objecthood, but rather between agency and instrumentality."

This is not tenable, because the imposition of contradictory attributes is equal [in both cases]; for there is a contradiction between agency and objecthood, but not between agency and being an agent.
Therefore, setting aside the fact that the self is grasped by the notion of "I," its status as a presiding controller alone is logically established.

Furthermore, even for those who maintain that the self— which they hold to be non-pervasive and equal in dimension to the body— is subject to transformation through the distinction between its substance and its cognitive modes (*paryāya*), their position is undermined by its own internal logic; for if it were subject to transformation, its nature as consciousness would be lost.
In the absence of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpatā), what would constitute the selfhood of the Self?
Therefore, by one who desires the selfhood of the Self, the nature of consciousness must necessarily be admitted;
and that [nature] is precisely the state of being the presiding subject (adhiṣṭhātṛtva).

Some maintain that the self is indeed of the nature of an agent; for instance, when an action characterized as cognition arises upon the proximity of an object, the result of that action is the consciousness of the object,
and within that consciousness which constitutes the result, the self's own nature appears in the form of luminosity.
The object exists as the apprehended and the self as the apprehender,
because that cognition arises in the form "I know the jar."
Since the agent alone is the cause of action, it follows that agency and enjoyership are the very nature of the self; however,
this is untenable because does that [self] attain agency over those cognitions simultaneously or sequentially?
If there were simultaneous agency, it would not have agency at any other moment;
if, on the other hand, agency occurs sequentially, that is not possible for something of a single nature.
If its agency were by means of a single form, then because that one [nature] is always present, every result would be of a single form.
If its agency consists in assuming various forms, then it would be subject to transformation;
and because of being subject to transformation, it could not possess the nature of consciousness.
Therefore, those who desire the self to be of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) should not accept direct agency (*sākṣātkartṛtva*);
rather, that very agency which we have established for the self—which is immutable, eternal, and of the nature of consciousness—is what is logically consistent.
By this, those who claim that the self, though self-luminous, manifests its status as a grasper (*grāhaka*) through the medium of the cognition of objects are also refuted.

Some who maintain that the self consists of consciousness by virtue of its nature as reflective awareness (vimarśa) say: "It is impossible to define the conscious nature of the self apart from reflective awareness;
indeed, the conscious nature is said to be nothing other than its distinction from the insentient."

And when that [object] is examined apart from reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it does not remain otherwise; that investigation— namely, the deliberation that "this is untenable" or "this has precisely this form"— is called reflective awareness.
Furthermore, that [cognition] does not even arise apart from *asmitā* (the sense of "I-am-ness").
To explain: the reflection (*vimarśa*) arising with respect to the self is experienced in the form "I am such-and-such.

Consequently, because the object characterized as the self—which is permeated by the word "I"—flashes forth therein, there is no transcendence of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in that case.
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), being of the nature of determination (*adhyavasāya*), is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*) and not a property of consciousness (*cit*).
Because consciousness is eternally uniform due to its immutable permanence, there can be no entry of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) into it.

Thus, by one who seeks to establish that the Self possesses self-reflective awareness (*savimarśatva*), it is merely the intellect that has been presented as the Self through delusion; the true nature of the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), whose essence is pure luminosity, has not been understood.
Thus, in all philosophical systems, no nature of the self is tenable apart from being a presiding agent; and this presiding agency is nothing other than the nature of consciousness,
which is precisely what distinguishes it from the insentient.

That which the conscious principle presides over by virtue of its nature as consciousness alone brings it to a state of being an object of experience; and that which is presided over by consciousness alone becomes fit for all functional activities.

This being the case, there is no other recourse for alternative philosophical systems than to abandon our stated doctrine of the soul’s isolation (*kaivalya*) upon the cessation of the activity of *pradhāna*, because of its eternity.

Therefore, this alone is rightly stated: Kaivalya (isolation) is the establishment of the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) in its own nature, free from the conformity with mental modifications (*vṛttisārūpya*).
All [beings] bow at the feet of that majestic abode, serving at the edge of his presence.
That illustrious Lord Bhoja, upon whose heads— the crowns of which were falling off— the lords of the earth place their commands,
and having attained whose lotus-face the Goddess of Speech has taken up an incomparable pride,
has composed a commentary on the *Patañjali-sūtras*.
